## Methods

Animals
Animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine in accordance with the guidelines and regulations of the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals (protocol #MO23K317). C57BL/6 wild-type mice (Mus musculus) were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (Jackson ID #000664); Cpt2lox/lox conditional mice from Dr. Michael J. Wolfgang63 (C57BL/6 genetic background) were bred to Nestin- or Gfap-Cre transgenic mice (Jackson ID #003771; B6.Cg-Tg(Nes-cre)1Kln/J and #024098; B6.Cg-Tg(Gfap-cre)77.6Mvs/2J) to generate pan-brain (Cpt2B−/−) or astrocyte-specific (Cpt2G−/−) knockout mice. Mice were bred in-house and the colonies maintained in the animal facility of Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in ventilated racks with a 12-hour light/dark cycle in a temperature (20-25°C) and humidity (30–70%) controlled room, and had ad libitum access to water and standard chow (5v75 - PicoLab Verified 75 IF, LabDiet).

Intermittent hypoxia
Postnatal day (P)1 pups were randomized to undergo intermittent hypoxia (IHx) or serve as normoxia (Nx) controls, removed from the dam, and placed in sealed containers (Coy Laboratories) at ambient temperature. IHx pups were exposed to 16 cycles of brief 3 min episodes of hypoxia (8% O2) followed by 5 min of re-oxygenation to 21% FiO2. Nx pups were exposed to 16 cycles of regular air. The pups were returned to their dam for 2h, and the 16 cycles of Nx or IHx were repeated. These 32 cycles in total were repeated daily for 11 days until P11. Pups from different litters and from both sexes were used for each experiment and were assessed at P11, P17, P22, and P30 unless otherwise stated. Data from males and females was reported as combined, male only, and female only. The hippocampus was selected a priori for microdissection and analysis due to its role in learning and memory, and its susceptibility to developmental disruption in children EPT. Blood glucose and lactate levels were determined using blood glucose and lactate meters (Nova Abbott). Blood was collected in 5% 0.5M EDTA, and plasma β-hydroxybutyrate (StanBio; 2440) and non-esterified fatty acids (NEFA) (Wako; 999-35691, 999-34791, 999-34891, 999-35191, 276-76491) were measured as per manufacturer’s instructions.

Glycerol-triacetate treatment
Normoxia and IHx-injured mice were randomized at P11 to receive vehicle (glycerol, Millipore Sigma; G5516) or glycerol-triacetate (Triacetin, Millipore Sigma; 1030001000). Glycerol or glycerol-triacetate was administered by oral gavage (5mg/g body weight) daily from P11 to P17.

Human samples
Human hippocampus was obtained from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) NeuroBioBank at University of Maryland, Baltimore, MD, United States (ID #3243). Donors consisted of ~1.6 months-old (average) infants born at term (38–40 weeks; n=4) and infants born extremely premature (≤28 weeks; n=3) with a corrected average age of ~1-month. Both sexes, male and female, were included in this study. None of the donors had a history of hypoxia ischemia, severe infection, or known genetic diseases. Frozen tissues were stored at –80°C.

Gene expression
Total RNA from microdissected hippocampal tissue (n=8/sex/age/group) was extracted using TRIzol (Life Technologies; 15596018), and further purified using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (Qiagen; 74134). RNA was quantified by NanoDrop One spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and converted to cDNA with the High Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcriptase kit (Applied Biosystems; 4368814). Real-Time PCR was performed using 10ng of cDNA, Sso Advanced Universal SYBR Green Supermix (Bio-Rad; 1725271), and primers for the target genes (Supplementary Table 18), and analyzed using the CFX Opus 96 machine (Bio-Rad). Data was normalized to the average Ct values of the housekeeping genes (18S, Ppia, Ywaz, and Osbp) and expressed as arbitrary units of 2-ΔCt.

To determine the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) content relative to nuclear DNA, genomic DNA was isolated from microdissected hippocampus using a QiAmp DNA Mini kit (Qiagen, #51304). EvaGreen-based digital PCR was performed by the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine Genetic Resources Core Facility (RRID:SCR_018669) using samples as a template and primers to amplify the mitochondrial target genes, cytochrome c oxidase I (Co1) and NADH dehydrogenase 1 (Nd1), and the nuclear target gene H19 (Supplementary Table 18). Biological replicates were tested in duplicate using an 8500 partition nanoplate (Qiagen #250021) in a QIAcuity 8; Firmware version 3.1 instrument (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s recommendations for EvaGreen. Each assay was run independently. Samples were run at 10ng/ul concentration for the H19 gene and at a 1:100 dilution for the mitochondrial genes. 5ul of the sample at the appropriate concentration was added to 7.2ul of master mix. 12.2ul of master mix was loaded into the nanoplate, and the instrument delivered 2.6ul of the total to be partitioned across each well. Results were analyzed with the QIAcuity Digital Suite v3.1.0.0 software (Qiagen). Concentrations were adjusted for all dilution levels within the software and are reported as copies/ul in the original 10ng/ul sample tube.

Proteomics
16-plex-TMTpro experiment was performed by the Johns Hopkins Mass Spectrometry and Proteomics Facility. Hippocampal protein was extracted from frozen microdissected hippocampal tissue (total n=16; n=4/sex/group; biological replicates) using RIPA lysis buffer system with protease inhibitors (Santa Cruz; sc-24948). The Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific; 23227) was used to determine protein concentration according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Proteolytic Digestion: Protein samples (50ug each) were diluted to 20ul with 50mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB), reduced with 5ul 50mM Dithiothreitol in 100mM TEAB at 60°C for 45min followed by alkylating with 100mM Chloroacetamide in 100mM TEAB in the dark for 15min at room temperature. A single pot, solid phase sample preparation protocol (SP3)64 using a mixture of Sera-Mag SpeedBeads (GE Healthcare; 45152105050250 and 65152105050250) was used to remove detergents and other non-protein contaminants. The proteins bound to beads were resuspended in 100ul of 100mM TEAB and digested with 3.4ug of Trypsin/LysC (Pierce) overnight at 37°C. The digested peptides were separated from the magnetic beads using a magnetic tube holder and placed into a new 0.5ml Eppendorf centrifuge tube. Isobaric Mass Tag Labeling: Peptides in each of the 16 digested samples were labeled with a unique TMTpro 16-plex reagent (Thermo Fisher; LOT# WH324722) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. All 16 TMT labeled peptide samples were combined and dried by vacuum centrifugation. Peptide fractionation: The combined TMT-labeled peptides (800ug) were aliquoted, and one aliquot of 300ug was dried prior to off-line fractionation. Peptides were re-constituted in 2ml 10mM TEAB buffer and loaded on a XBridge C18 Guard Column (5µm, 2.1×10mm, Waters) at 250µL/min for 8min prior to fractionation on a XBridge C18 Column (5µm, 2.1×100mm column (Waters) using a 0 to 90% acetonitrile in 10mM TEAB gradient over 85min at 250µL/min on an Agilent 1200 series capillary HPLC with a micro-fraction collector. Eighty-four 250ul fractions were collected and concatenated into 24 fractions according to Wang et al. 2011 and dried65. Mass Spectrometry analysis: Peptides in each of the 24 fractions were analyzed on a nano-LC-Orbitrap-Fusion Lumos-IC in FTFT mode (Thermo Fisher Scientific) interfaced with an EasyLC 1100 series by reversed-phase chromatography using a 2%–90% acetonitrile in 0.1% formic acid gradient over 90min at 300nl/min on a 75µm×150mm ReproSIL-Pur-120-C18-AQ column 3µm, 120Å (Dr. Maisch). Survey scans of precursor ions were acquired from 375 to 1500m/z at 120,000 resolution at 200m/z with automatic gain control (AGC) at 4e5 and a 50ms maximum injection time. Precursor ions were individually isolated in a 3 second cycle time within 0.7m/z by data dependent monitoring and 15s dynamic exclusion, and fragmented using an HCD activation collision energy 36. Fragmentation spectra (MS/MS) were acquired using a 1.25e5 AGC and 86ms maximum injection time (IT) at 50,000 resolution. Data analysis: Fragmentation spectra were processed by Proteome Discoverer v2.4 (PD2.4, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and searched with Mascot v.2.8.0 (Matrix Science, London, UK) against RefSeq 2021_204 mouse database. Search criteria included trypsin enzyme, one missed cleavage, 3ppm precursor mass tolerance, 0.01Da fragment mass tolerance, with TMTpro on N-terminus and carbamidomethylation on C as fixed and TMTpro on K, oxidation on M, deamidation on N or Q as variable modifications. Peptide identifications from the Mascot searches were processed within PD2.4 using Percolator at a 5% False Discovery Rate confidence threshold, based on an auto-concatenated decoy database search. Peptide spectral matches (PSMs) were filtered for Isolation Interference <30%. Relative protein abundances of identified proteins were determined in PD2.4 from the normalized median ratio of TMT reporter ions, having signal to noise ratios >1.5, from all PSMs from the same protein. P-values of mean protein ratios for the biological replicates were calculated using the ANOVA method. Technical variation in ratios from our mass spectrometry analysis is less than 10%66. Pathway enrichment analysis: Pathway analysis of differentially expressed proteins (p-value <0.05) was performed using g:Profiler (https://biit.cs.ut.ee/gprofiler/gost). g:SCS was selected as statistical threshold and p-value <0.05 as the significance threshold. Significant pathways from Reactome were selected and the pathways belonging to the first or second hierarchical levels were plotted67. The proteomics data generated in this study have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE68 partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD070491.

Behavior
Novel object recognition (NOR) test and Y-Maze spontaneous alternation test. Novel object recognition test: The test was used to assess hippocampal-dependent recognition memory and performed as previously described in ref. 69. In brief, the open field and objects used were always cleaned with 30% ethanol (vol/vol) between each mouse to minimize olfactory cues. Prior to the testing day, P30 mice were habituated to an opaque rectangular box (27×27×20cm) for 5min. In the familiarization phase, mice were placed inside the box and allowed to explore two identical objects, placed equidistant from each other, for a total of 30s or after 5min had passed. The test was repeated 12h later but one object was replaced with a novel object. Mice were placed inside the box and allowed to explore the objects. The experiment stopped when the mouse explored the objects for a total of 30s. The time it took to reach the criterion of 30s and the total time spent exploring each individual object were recorded and analyzed with the ANY-maze video tracking system (v6.3, Stoelting Co., IL). The recognition index was calculated by dividing the amount of time spent on the novel object by the total exploration time (Time in novel / 30sec). Y-Maze spontaneous alternation test: The test was used to assess spatial working memory as previously described in refs. 69, 70. In brief, P30 mice were placed in the center of a Y-shaped maze and allowed to freely explore the three arms (labeled as A, B, and C) for 8 minutes. The activity and arm choice were recorded with a video camera. The Y-maze was cleaned with 30% ethanol (v/v) between mice. The spontaneous alternation percentage was calculated by dividing the number of alternations (three unique arm entries) by the total number of possible triads minus one (Total alternations/[total entries–2]) × 100. All behavioral tests were performed by the investigator blinded to groups and treatments.

Mito Fuel Flex test
The Mito Fuel Flex test (Agilent) was performed using a Seahorse XFe96 analyzer (Agilent) to measure the dependency of brain cells to oxidize glucose, glutamine, and fatty acids to maintain basal respiration. Single-cell suspensions from microdissected hippocampus were prepared using accutase. The Agilent Seahorse Technical Manual was followed to determine the rate of oxidation of each fuel by measuring the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) in the presence or absence of inhibitors for each of the specific fuel pathways. UK5099 was used as an inhibitor of glucose oxidation, etomoxir as an inhibitor of fatty acid oxidation, and BPTES as an inhibitor of glutamine oxidation. All assays were performed and analyzed in real-time by the manufacturer’s software (Wave 2.6.3). The number of cells plated was analyzed with Biotek Cytation 1 (Agilent), and OCR was normalized to protein concentration in each well. The protein concentration was exported directly to the Agilent Seahorse, and raw data was normalized to account for differences in protein concentration within each well.

Lipidomics
Frozen mouse microdissected hippocampal tissue or human hippocampal tissue (Mouse tissue-total n=48; n=6/age/group, biological replicates; human tissue – total n=7, term/control n=4, preterm n=3; biological replicates) were homogenized with PBS buffer at a concentration 100mg/ml. The total lipid extracts of the brain tissue were prepared using a revised MTBE lipid extraction method71. Briefly, 10ul of brain homogenate, 400ul of ice-cold methanol, and 10ul of internal standard (EquiSPLASH, Avanti Polar Lipids, Alabaster, AL) were combined, vortex mixed for 30s, and then incubated at 4°C for 10min with 650rpm shaking. Next, 500ul of ice-cold MTBE was added, vortex mixed for 30s and incubated at 4°C for 1h with 650rpm shaking. After incubation, 500ul of ice-cold H2O was added, vortex mixed for 30s and incubated at 4°C for 15min with 650rpm shaking. The mixture was then centrifuged at 8000g for 8min at 4°C, and the top organic layer was collected and stored on ice. An additional 200ul of MTBE was added to the aqueous phase, vortex mixed for 30s, incubated at 4°C for 15min, and centrifuged at 8000g for 8min at 4°C. The organic layer was collected and combined with the previous extract. The collected organic layer was dried under N2 gas and re-suspended in 200ul of CHCl3/MeOH (1:1, v/v) containing 200uM of butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) and stored at −20°C until analysis. Samples were further diluted with IPA/ACN/H2O (2:1:1 v/v) prior to analysis. The total protein content was measured with a Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Rockford, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol, and used for the data normalization.

The liquid chromatography, tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis was conducted on an Ultimate 3000 Ultra High-Performance Liquid Chromatograph (UHPLC) coupled to a Thermo TSQ Altis Tandem Quadrupole Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Scientific, San Jose, CA). Chromatographic separation was achieved with an ACQUITY Amide BEH column (1.7μm, 2.1×100mm) maintained at 45°C (Waters, Milford, MO). Mobile phase compositions for solvents A and B consisted of ACN/H2O (95:5, v/v) and (50:50, v/v) respectively, with 10mM ammonium acetate. The gradient profile had a flow rate of 0.6ml min−1 and ramped from 0.1 to 20% B in 2min, from 20 to 80% B in 3min, dropped from 80 to 0.1% B in 0.1min, and held 0.1% B for 2.9min. Total chromatographic run time was 8.0min. The injection volume was 2ul. All analytes were detected using negative or positive ionization mode and selection reaction monitoring (SRM) library were adopted from Medina et al.72. The SRM is a targeted method that uses predetermined chromatographic retention times and precursor-to-production transitions to detect and identify each lipid, and has been implemented in our previously published studies73–75. Data were acquired using spiked-in internal standards (Avanti Polar Lipids EquiSPLASH, #330731) which provided one deuterium stable-labeled lipid per lipid class. The lipid standards allowed for compensation during lipid extraction and ionization efficiency. Collision energies and RF lens voltage were optimized for each reference standard. Data acquisition was performed using Xcalibur software v4.2 (Thermo Scientific, San Jose, CA) and processed using TraceFinder 5.1 (Thermo Scientific, San Jose, CA). Peak area was determined using ICIS peak peaking algorithm and 7-point smoothing. All peak area integration was manually verified. The peaks areas were then normalized to sum composition, mean-centered, and log-transformed using MetaboAnalyst 6.0 (https://www.metaboanalyst.ca/)76. The data as presented represent abundances rather than concentrations, enabling visualizing of hundreds of detected lipids with multivariate and univariate statistical analyses. Additional data analysis was done using MetaboAnalyst 6.0 and Prism 10 (GraphPad, La Jolla, CA). The lipidomics data generated in this study have been deposited in the Mendeley Data Repository under the https://doi.org/10.17632/nzwvkr7vgj.177.

Total Lipid Fatty Acid Analyses
Chemicals, reagents, and materials used for the lipid extractions and fatty acid analyses were of the highest quality available. MilliQ water, filtered deionized water is available in the laboratory. Methanol, optima grade was obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Fair Lawn, NJ). Chloroform, HPLC grade was from Burdick & Jackson (Muskegan, MI), Stable-isotope-labeled internal standards (deuterated); were purchased from Cambridge Isotope Laboratories, Andover MA (internal standards C27:0 and C19:0; deuterium fatty acids, C8:0, 10:0, 12:0, 14:0, 15:0, 16, 18:0, 20:0, 22:0) or CDN Isotopes, Quebec, CAN (deuterium fatty acids C24:0, 26:0, pristanic and phytanic). Natural fatty acid standards were purchased from Nu Chek Prep (Elysian, MN) and were checked for purity by capillary gas chromatography by analysis on two capillary columns, a non-polar, DB1, and a polar, SP2560, capillary columns (50m×0.25mm×0.2µm) purchased from Supelco, Sigma-Aldrich, Inc, St. Louis, MO.

Frozen microdissected hippocampal tissues (total n=142; P11: male Nx n=4, IHx n=5, female Nx n=6, IHx n=5; P17: male Nx n=5, IHx n=6, female Nx n=6, IHx n=7; P22: male Nx n=6, IHx n=5, female n=6/group; P30: n=6/sex/group; P30 glycerol/glycerol-triacetate experiment-male: Nx glycerol n=6, Nx glycerol-triacetate n=5, IHx glycerol n=5, IHx glycerol-triacetate n=7; female: Nx glycerol n=6, Nx glycerol-triacetate n=6, IHx glycerol n=6, IHx glycerol-triacetate n=10; biological replicates) were weighed (0.1 to 0.2 g) and extracted with chloroform:methanol 2:1, v/v according to Folch et al.78. Total lipids were dried under N2 and weighed. The lipids were solubilized in 1ml chloroform:methanol 2:1, and approximately 1mg lipid from each sample was transferred to a 13x100mm screw capped test tube for analysis of total lipid fatty acids, including saturated, monounsaturated, and polyunsaturated of chain length C10 to C30. Fatty acids were hydrolyzed from triglycerides and phospholipids in a two-step process of acidification with 90:10v:v acetonitrile:6N HCl and neutralization with 90:10v:v methanol:10N NaOH, with incubations at 104°C for 45min, then reacidified in 6N HCl. Total fatty acids were extracted in hexane then derivatized with triethylamine and pentafluorobenzyl bromide (in acetonitrile) at room temperature 15min79,80. The resulting pentaflourobenzyl bromide esters were separated and quantified by capillary gas chromatography electron capture negative ion mass spectrometry (GCMS) by the method of Lagerstedt et al.81 except that a 50m×0.25mm×0.2µm SP2560 column was used for analysis. All fatty acids were analyzed on an Agilent 7890A GC coupled to a 5975C mass selective detector (MSD), with helium as the carrier gas and ammonia as the reagent gas. After a 1µl 1:35 split injection, the oven temperature was ramped more slowly at lower temperatures in two steps, resulting in a total run time of 55min. The initial oven temperature of 60°C was held for 2min, then increased at 10°C/min to 180°C, followed by a slower ramp at 2.5°C/min to 250°C, and then held for 14min. The MSD transfer line was initially maintained at 240°C for 33minutes, then increased at 2.5°C/min to a final temperature of 250°C and held for an additional 32min. Data were acquired in selection monitoring (SIM) mode, with dwell times ranging from 50ms to 100ms per ion species. Each analyte was matched to one of 13 stable-isotope labeled internal standards with the closest chain length and retention time. The fatty acids were quantitated using the Agilent MSD ChemStation software G1701EA version E.02.02.1431. The fatty acid retention time and peak integration were checked and each fatty acid was measured using a standard curve that was assayed with each set of analyses. For quality control, a reagent blank, a normal, and an abnormal plasma control samples were assayed with each set of analyses. Results were transferred into Excel for the final calculations as fatty acid ug/mg lipid weight.

Acylcarnitines
Acylcarnitines levels in the blood (total n=62; male: P11, P17, and P22 n=4/group; P30 Nx n=4, IHx, n=5; female: P11 Nx n=4, IHx n=3; P17 n=4/group; P22 Nx n=4, IHx, n=3; P30 Nx n=3, IHx, n=4; biological replicates) were quantified from dried blood spots (DBS) following a previously described method with modifications3,4. In brief, punched 1/8″ DBS samples were transferred into tubes containing 100ul of methanol and internal standards for acylcarnitines (NSKB; Cambridge Isotopes). Samples were incubated at 4°C for 20min and then dried under nitrogen. The dried samples were resuspended in 60μl 3N HCl in n-butanol and incubated at 65°C for 15min. Afterward, samples were dried under nitrogen and the residue containing butylated acylcarnitines was reconstituted in 100ul of mobile phase acetonitrile/water/formic acid (H2O:CH3CN:HCOOH; 80:19.9:0.1v/v%). Samples were vortexed, transferred to a centrifuge filter, and spun. The filtrates were then transferred to injection vials.

Acylcarnitines from frozen hippocampus (total n=63; male: P11, P17, and P22 n=4/group; P30 Nx n=4, IHx, n=5; female: P11 Nx n=5, IHx n=3; P17 n=4/group; P22 Nx n=4, IHx, n=3; P30 Nx n=3, IHx, n=4; biological replicates) were extracted by homogenizing the tissue in a solution of methanol containing the acylcarnitine standards. Samples were sonicated at room temperature for 10min and then centrifuged at 16,200×g for 4min at 4°C. After centrifugation, the liquid phase was transferred to a glass tube, evaporated under nitrogen, and processed as described above. Analysis of acylcarnitines was performed using an API 4500 mass spectrometer (AB SCIEX, Foster City, CA) operated in the positive-ion mode employing precursor ion scan for m/z 85, a characteristic production of butyl ester of acylcarnitine species. Data was processed using the ChemoView 2.0.2 (AB SCIEX) application. Blood samples are reported as nmol/ml and tissue samples as pmol/mg.

MALDI-MSI
MALDI MSI experiments were performed by the Johns Hopkins Applied Imaging Mass Spectrometry (AIMS) Core. All solvents and MALDI matrices were purchased from Sigma Aldrich (St. Louis, MO) and were used without further purification. All solvents were of HPLC grade or higher. Sample preparation: Brain samples from Nx and IHx P17 male mice were collected immediately after sacrifice and frozen using liquid nitrogen vapors (total n=8; n=4/group). Samples were stored at −80°C before cryosectioning. 10µm thick sagittal brain sections were collected using a Leica CM1860 UV Cryostat (Leica Biosystems, Wetzlar, Germany) and depth was verified by comparing tissue morphology to Allen Brain Atlas images at the target depth. Sections were thaw-mounted onto indium-tin oxide (ITO) coated glass microscope slides (Delta Technologys, Loveland, CO) and stored at −80°C prior to matrix application. Matrix application: Slides were warmed to room temperature in a vacuum desiccator, then sprayed with 5mg/mL α-cyano-4-hydroxycinnamic acid (CHCA) in 70% acetonitrile with 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid using an HTX M3+ pneumatic matrix sprayer (HTX Technologies, Chapel Hill, NC). Matrix was sprayed at 100µL/min for 8 passes using a 60°C nozzle temperature, 10psi nitrogen pressure, 1350mm/min nozzle velocity, 3mm track spacing, and 10second drying time. MALDI-MSI data acquisition: Immediately after matrix deposition, slides were imaged using a Bruker timsTOF fleX MALDI-2 mass spectrometer (Bruker Daltonics, Billerica, MA) equipped with a SmartBeam 3D 10kHz Nd:YAG laser at 355nm with beam scan enabled and a 46um scan range. Height adjustment and laser focus tuning were performed prior to mass calibration. Mass calibration was performed using electrospray ionization (ESI) of Agilent ESI-L Tune Mix, resulting in a mass error <1 PPM. Instrument parameters were optimized to maximize intensity, as described in Supplementary Table 19. Data were acquired for m/z 100–950 in positive ion mode using a 50µm raster width with 1 burst of 225 laser shots per pixel. On-tissue MS/MS analysis was conducted by switching the instrument to MS/MS mode and collecting 5 summed bursts of 250 shots from the hippocampus of Nx and IHx samples for the parent and fragment spectra of each species of interest (Supplementary Figs. 10, 11). Parent ions were searched against the Lipid Maps database82–84. MALDI MSI data analysis: MALDI MSI data were imported into SCiLS Lab (version 2023b, Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, Germany). Data were normalized using total ion current (TIC) and analyzed using SCiLS lab’s feature finding and hypothesis testing workflows.

In-vivo metabolite uptake
Glucose uptake into the brain was measured using [1,2-3H]-2-Deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG) (Moravek Biochemicals; MT911), an unmetabolizable analog of glucose that enters cells but becomes trapped after phosphorylation. Mice were injected intraperitoneal (i.p.) with 0.2uCi/g of 2-DG diluted in sterile saline. Brains were harvested 45minutes after injection. Tissue from microdissected hippocampus was extracted using ice-cold 7% perchloric acid and centrifuged at 14,000g for 15min at 4°C. The supernatant was transferred to a vial containing scintillation fluid (National Diagnostics; LS-270) and radioactivity was measured in a LS 6500 Multi-purpose Scintillation Counter (Beckman Counter, Inc. USA). Disintegrations per minute (DPM) counts were normalized to wet tissue weight.

Fatty acid uptake into the hippocampus was measured using [1-14C]-2-Bromopalmitate (2-BP, Moravek Biochemicals; MC451). Mice were injected intraperitoneal (i.p.) with 0.2uCi/g of 2-BP complexed to bovine serum albumin and diluted in sterile saline. Microdissected hippocampus were harvested 45minutes after injection. Total lipids were extracted using the Folch method and transferred to vials containing scintillation liquid to measure radioactivity in a LS 6500 Multi-purpose Scintillation Counter (Beckman Counter, Inc. USA)78. DPM counts for 14C were normalized to wet tissue weight.

Ex-vivo oxidation studies
Oxidation assays were measured in stoppered tubes containing a center well with Whatman filter paper as previously described in refs. 3, 4, 85. In brief, the hippocampal region was microdissected and placed into tubes with labeling media containing either [1-14C]-oleic acid (Moravek Biochemicals; MC406), [U-14C]-D-glucose (Moravek Biochemicals; MC144W), [U-14C]-glutamine (Moravek Biochemicals; MC1124), [U-14C]-L-lactic acid (PerkinElmer; NEC599050UC), [3-14C]-D-3-Hydroxybutyric acid, (American Radiolabeled Chemicals, Inc; ARC#4122), or [1,2-14C]-acetic acid (PerkinElmer; NEC553050UC) and incubated in a 37°C water bath with gentle shaking for 3h. Labeling media was composed of 20% neurobasal medium (Gibco; 21103-049), 80% DMEM (Gibco; A14430), 0.5mM L-carnitine (Sigma; C0283), 0.2% bovine serum albumin (BSA; Sigma; A9647), and 25μM glutamine (Gibco; 25030). 100μM Etoximir (Sigma; E1905) was added to the media of the treated samples at the beginning of the assay as control for the [1-14C]-oleic acid oxidation assay. 14CO2 from complete substrate oxidation was trapped by the addition of 200μl of 1M perchloric acid in the medium and 150μl of 1M NaOH to the center well containing the filter paper and incubating the samples at 55°C for 1hour. The filter paper was transferred to a vial containing scintillation fluid and the radioactivity was counted 24h later. 1ml of acidified media was collected to measure acid-soluble metabolites, products from incomplete [1-14C]-oleic acid oxidation. 60μl of BSA and 100ul of 1M perchloric acid were added to the media and incubated overnight at 4°C. The next day, samples were centrifuged at 1467×g for 30min, the supernatant was transferred to vials containing scintillation fluid, and radioactivity was measured in a LS 6500 Multi-purpose Scintillation Counter (Beckman Counter, Inc. USA). DPM counts for 14CO2 and 14C-ASM were normalized to specific activity and wet tissue weight.

Lipid synthesis
Acetate incorporation into total lipid fraction was performed using [3H]-Acetate85,86. The microdissected hippocampal region was incubated at 37°C for 3h with 1uCi [3H]-Acetate (Moravek Biochemicals; MT634) in the same media composition used for the oxidation assays. Total lipids were extracted using the Folch method and transferred to vials containing scintillation fluid to measure radioactivity in a LS 6500 Multi-purpose Scintillation Counter (Beckman Counter, Inc. USA)78. DPM counts for 3H were normalized to wet tissue weight.

Data and statistical analysis
Data are shown as the mean ± SEM for each group unless otherwise stated. Data were analyzed using Prism 10 software (GraphPad, La Jolla, CA). Additional data analysis was performed using MetaboAnalyst 6.076. The statistical significance was determined using the 2-tailed Mann–Whitney test or unpaired Student’s t-test at instances where the total sample size was ≤7, 2-tailed paired t-test, and 2-way ANOVA with uncorrected Fisher’s LSD post-hoc. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05. Correlation analysis was performed using simple linear regression.

Artwork
Experimental design figures and biochemical pathways figures were created with BioRender.com full license plan.

Reporting summary
Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

General comments:
In this study, Fernandez et al. investigated the impact of brain intermittent hypoxemia during neonatal stage on lipid
metabolism. Using a mouse model of neonatal brain injury due to intermittent hypoxemia, the authors reported that it led to
cognitive impairments later in life. They also demonstrated that post-natal intermittent hypoxemia led to an alteration of lipid
profile signatured mainly by decreased levels of very long-chain fatty acids, which was associated with
enhanced mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation. The authors also demonstrated that acetate treatment can promote functional recovery by
sparing fatty acid oxidation.
The topic of investigation is novel and of high significance, the authors also performed a comprehensive study with logical
design, which led to conclusions that could potentially be of clinical relevance. There are several considerations necessary
to solidify their central conclusions, including verification of findings in human samples, justification of model used,
discussion of potential sex differences, and interpretation of mechanism related to the altered lipid metabolism.
Major comments:
1. The study has been performed in a mouse IHx model. Although the study timeline was well-designed, whether this model
closely resembles EPT neonatal hypoxia-induced brain injury demands further justification.
a) There are studies (e.g., PMID 33984336) reported that the age point as well as the interval of hypoxia treatment regimen
can lead to either impaired or improved memory function, the authors should provide literature support regarding the basis of
IHx model set up in this study.
b) Given the importance of time frame of IHx poses on the outcome, and the fact that IHx in human infant started preterm
(EPT birth), this model is using a full term born mouse model to mimic post birth IHx, whether this could cause a difference in
the lipid or protein profile needs to be considered/discussed.
2. The authors have demonstrated astrocyte as the major source of the increased fatty acid oxidation (FAO) after IHx using
an astrocyte-specific CPT2 ko mouse model. This may align with the fact that astrocytes are the main cell for lipid
metabolism and function as a supporter for neurons. However, myelination is also in high demand during post-natal stage,
and myelin is well-known to be highly-enriched in VLCFA. In Fig.1G, multiple top-altered lipid species are cerebrosides
(Hex1Cer, Hex2Cer) that are specifically abundant in myelin sheaths. The possibility of potential contribution of
oligodendrocytes to the altered lipid profile under IHx condition should be re-evaluated and discussed.
3. In concordance with Fig.1G which showed top lipid changes on P30, it would be informative to provide lipid species
alteration data on P17 in Figure 3.
4. As P11 is immediately after the IHx treatment, this would be a critical time point for any lipid change evaluation. In line
with this, Fig. S5B-D showed that P11 has a transient AC elevation in the IHx hippocampus. More comprehensive lipidomic
analysis should be provided at this time point, as it is important for understanding of events happened during and
immediately after IHx.
5. P30 is still a relatively young age to make conclusion about potential long-term impact of IHx, lipid profile data from more
aged groups (with neonatal IHx) would be helpful to evaluate the significance of IHx impact.
6. Data from Fig.1G showed that total CL (cardiolipin) levels were decreased in the IHx group. As CL plays a critical role in
mitochondrial morphology, bioenergetics, dynamics, and signaling, have the authors noticed any differences between IHx
and Nx in aspects such as mitochondrial number, quality, capacity, as well as tissue ATP levels (especially at P11)? These
measurements and discussions will be important for interpreting findings of this study.
7. The authors should be cautious in interpretating results from Fig. 3D. Data with sodium adduct in addition to potassium
adduct should be provided to rule out the possibility of ion- vs. lipid- distribution resulted observation. Alternatively, this
figure could be removed.
8. The authors have well-organized multiple aspects of their findings in main figures combining both sexes and displayed
further sex-specific data in supplemental figures. While most of the findings showed similar trend between male and
females, some observations show sex-specific patterns (e.g., Fig. S3B-C, Fig. S4C). Whether there are sex differences on
the long-term impact of EPT among humans, and whether the conclusions of this study have any sex discrepancy
should be discussed.
9. Based on data from proteomics and mRNA levels (Fig.2C-D, and Fig. S7), it appears lipid metabolism (both fatty acid
synthesis and oxidation) pathways were down-regulated at P11 post IHx. Meanwhile, Mito Fuel functional test indicated
increased fatty acid oxidation (Fig. 3A). This contradiction should be further explained. The authors should be cautious in
interpretation of the [1-14C]-oleic acid as it only represents the oxidation of the first carbon (14C) and does not fully represent
the FAO activity overall.
10. Fig. 2B showed both TCA and ETC proteins were down-regulated at P11, this is an understandable outcome of the
decreased oxygen availability during IHx. Considering that the shutdown of TCA and ETC itself may be sufficient to cause
accumulation of intermediate metabolites of up-stream FAO, whether the enhanced AC levels at P11 is due to increased
FAO activity, or due to shutdown of ETC is questionable, which leads an incomplete FAO and AC
accumulation.
11. The study in mouse model is comprehensive, yet the study lacks verification of its findings in human samples/models.
Considering the difficulty of acquiring human infant brain samples, some of the findings from this study could potentially be
verified using samples from brain tissues of post-mortem infant who has experienced hypoxia (for example, hypoxic
ischemic encephalopathy infant cases are available from NIH NeuroBioBank). Also, some of the findings in blood samples
can be easily verified in human.
Minor comments:
1. Line 104 “reduction in fatty acids” does not seem to be accurate, as both reduction of very long-chain fatty acids (C22:0, C23:0,……),
and increase of other fatty acids (C16:0, C20:4) were observed.
2. The title should specify intermittent hypoxemia-induced neonatal brain injury, as neonatal brain injury may involve other
aspects/causes.

### Reviewer 3

Summary
Fernandez et al. extensively addressed an existing gap in the literature surrounding changes in brain lipid metabolism and
the brain lipid profile in infants born extremely preterm (i.e. less than 28 weeks gestation following brain injury). Authors used
an established model of neonatal brain injury by subjecting mice to intermittent hypoxia (IHx) via episodes of hypoxia (32
cycles) from P0-P11, alongside an arm of normoxia (Nx) controls. Male, and female pups from different litters
were used for the majority of experimentation at P11, P17, P22 and P30.
Authors examined the mouse hippocampus following injury and found that there was no change between IHx and Nx groups
in total hippocampal lipids, however, changes in lipid composition were found that were in-part, sex-specific. Namely, at
P30, males had significantly lower hippocampal omega 9 fatty acids (n-9), while palmitic acid (16:0; PAM) and arachidonic
acid (20:4n-6; ARA) were significantly increased in IHx compared to Nx. In both sexes, very long chain fatty acids (VLCFA; >
or equal to 20 carbons) were significantly decreased in IHx compared to Nx. Interestingly, PAM, the primary product of DNL
was the top differentially expressed fatty acid (FA) between IHx and Nx groups in males at P30.
Based on changes in hippocampal lipid composition, authors sought to rule out if these changes were a result of altered
nutrient supply following hypoxic injury. After measuring hippocampal glucose uptake, circulating NEFA levels, plasma
ketones and acyl-carnitines, and hippocampal acyl-carnitines, it was concluded that the change in hippocampal lipid
composition was not a result of a limited supply of nutrients following injury. This led authors to conduct an unbiased
proteomics analysis of the hippocampus at P11, in order to identify proteins and pathways responsible for the altered lipid
composition following IHx. Postnatal day 11 was selected for proteomics because at this timepoint, plasma levels of ketones
and acyl-carnitines were increased in IHx compared to Nx groups, and this corresponded to increased hippocampal acyl-
carnitines – giving insight to FAs being mobilized for the generation of acetyl-coA.
At P11, pathway analysis of proteomics data revealed the downregulation of multiple pathways involved in the metabolism
of lipids in the IHx group; specifically, the downregulation of genes involved in FA oxidation (cpt2), the synthesis of long
chain FA and cholesterol (scd2), lipid regulators (acc1), and FASN. However, these changes were transient and recovered
by P30 (for example, FASN was downregulated at P11, and became upregulated by P30).
Authors then sought to address functional changes resulting from alterations in hippocampal lipid composition by assessing
the dependency of the hippocampus on different metabolic fuels. Using a seahorse mito fuel flex test kit; validated by
measuring the oxidation of substrates labelled with 14C, authors found that metabolic brain fuels utilized depend on time.
Specifically, the injured brain depends more on the oxidation of glucose at P11 only, while FA oxidation was high at P11,
and 6 days post injury (P17).
Because the hippocampal oxidation of FA remained high post-injury at P17, authors sought to determine if the brain also
had an increase in circulating FA uptake. Using an analogue of PAM that cannot be metabolized (3H-2-bromopalmitate),
authors found a significant increase in FA uptake in IHx mice compared to Nx, alongside unchanged 14C-glutamine, -BHB
and -lactate uptakes at P17 between IHx and Nx. Authors concluded based on this result, that following
hypoxia, from P11 to recovery (P17), the brain upregulates FA oxidation to fuel and support
oxidative metabolism.
Since FA were extensively oxidized up until P17, authors then sought to measure the FA profile of the hippocampus at P17.
In both sexes, n-9 and total saturated fatty acids (SFAs) (> 20 carbons – which accumulate during development and are
extensively synthesized) were significantly lower in IHx compared to Nx groups. Authors further characterized these
changes in situ using non targeted MS imaging in multiple brain regions, as well as in a conditional KO mouse of CPT2.
Together, these experiments showed IHx results in hippocampal region-specific lipid changes
(corroborating the total lipid fatty acid profile at P17), and astrocytes are the primary brain cells
that oxidize FAs.
Lastly, and arguably most importantly, authors tested acetate treatment in a) the media and b) in vivo to investigate if acetate
supply would spare FA from oxidation (using oleic acid; 18:1n-9; OLA). Authors found treating the media with glucose to
spare FA from oxidation did not impact OLA oxidation, however, OLA oxidation in the presence of acetate decreased by
86% and 93% at P11, and P17, respectively, in IHx compared to Nx. Next, authors found in-vivo acetate treatment (glycerol-
triacetate to pups by oral gavage; 5mg/g birth weight) daily from P11-P17 reduced 14C-OLA oxidation by 71% at P17
compared to glycerol (vehicle) in the IHx group. Authors found in-vivo treatment with acetate also resulted in improved
recognition indexes in the Novel Object Recognition (NOR) test performed at the later timepoint of P30; suggesting an
improvement in recognition memory in addition to sparing FA from oxidation.
Altogether, Fernandez et al. employed exhaustive approaches to investigate and characterize
alterations following injury in the developing brain. As beta-oxidation is usually negligible in the developing brain, this data provides novel evidence that
is not the case following neonatal injury, where beta-oxidation is significantly upregulated. This metabolic shift results in a
decreased VLCFA content in the brain, and interestingly, impacts cognitive performance (at P30) – in which
sparing FA from oxidation can improve neurologic outcomes (the opposite to what is observed in
adulthood, in which increased oxidation is associated with improved cognitive performance).
Importantly, this paper demonstrates the unique specificity of the injured brain with regards to
substrates utilized for oxidative metabolism during development, and results are promising for
beginning to investigate effective treatments following neonatal brain injury.
Specific comments:
Major comments:
1. Palmitic acid is the primary product of de novo lipogenesis (DNL) and happens to be identified in males at P30 as the top
differentially expressed FA in your volcano plot (Fig 1H; p < 0.001) between IHx and Nx groups, which is consistent with IHx
males having a significantly higher hippocampal PAM at P30 than Nx males. Could DNL be increasing in your IHx group in
attempt to maintain brain energy requirements and/or FA balance in PL in response to injury? Especially since FASN (the
major governor of DNL) was also upregulated at P30 in IHx males? Not a lot of discussion/hypotheses around this result,
which also appears to be sex-specific.
2. Almost all results shown are limited to the hippocampus, and not the whole brain (other than the MS imaging data). How
might you predict your findings to change at the level of the whole brain, or other regions? If hippocampus was important a
priori this could be mentioned.
3. Authors state there is a “reduction” in brain lipids in the abstract and elsewhere, however, total lipids in the hippocampus
(primary region examined) are unchanged between IHx and Nx groups (% of total lipids per mg of tissue). Rather, it is lipid
composition which changed. Language needs to be 1) altered to reflect this is not a real “reduction”, and 2) clarify this result
is region-specific.
4. Presenting hippocampal lipid composition data in a supplemental table – as both concentration and relative %,
would be useful to the reader.
5. There is an overall lack of justification surrounding why the hippocampus was selected for analyses (see comment
above), besides the obvious reason it corresponds to behavioural analyses conducted. Is the hippocampus equipped for
oxidation compared to others? Lipid synthesis? This could be explained better.
6. Pups were removed from the dam for extended periods of time very early in development to undergo cycles of hypoxia (16
x 3 min hypoxia + 5 min re-oxygenation x 2 = 32 cycles). This is a significant amount of time, and enough to impact maternal
stress. Did authors measure and/or consider maternal stress, and if this can program pups postnatally?
7. This is a lot of assays for a very small brain tissue to undergo. A supplemental table outlining which pups underwent
which assay would aid in the reader understanding the results better. Furthermore, the use of “mice” throughout the methods
should specify the age, and sex of the mice as authors used many timepoints and both sexes.
8. Were any other tissues collected from these mice? It would be nice to see the FA composition of a peripheral tissue like
the liver and rule out if total lipids changed in peripheral tissues, but not the brain. Perhaps there is between-tissue FA
exchange to maintain total brain FAs.
9. IHx group weighs significantly less than Nx at most timepoints in both sexes. I understand this is necessary to model
extremely preterm infants, however, this could also impact overall metabolism, and substrates used for energy. Are
hippocampal lipid alterations a result of hypoxia, weight loss, or both?
Minor comments:
1. Abstract: The abstract overall is a bit boilerplate for the results described. Adding more detail to the results with regards to
timepoints, sex, etc. would better capture your findings.
2. Abstract: Line 109: “timely” supply – again, we know this is a critical period of brain development but what exactly are the
timepoints that the intervention (triacetin) would have the most benefit?
3. Introduction: line 143: provide a citation for IHx as clinically relevant model of neonatal brain injury?
4. Introduction: line 147: “clinically feasible source of acetate” – provide more detail supporting why this is clinically feasible?
I assume it has a bitter taste; it is recognized safe as a food additive but what dose would it need to be administered as, and
would this be GRAS?
5. Language around timepoints selected and interpretation:
a. Line 153-154: the “neonatal period” authors selected not only impacts what would be a premature infant (PND 1-2/3 in a
mouse), but also the window of a term infant (PND 7-10 mouse) – translationally, are children that are born extremely
preterm exposed to intermittent hypoxia as a term infant, as well?
b. By P30 in a mouse, the brain is 90-95% of adult weight and corresponds to what would be a 2-3 year old child. Be careful
with language around this timepoint referring to “later” in life.
6. Figure 1B-D and Extended Figure 1A-B: Add units for x-axis (i.e. “day 30” or “P30”). It is unclear what units you are
referring to.
7. Figure 1E-F: Inconsistency in naming of PC 1/2 – pick either PC or component.
8. I would consider adding the differentially expressed fatty acid data for females into the figure with males, as it is equally as
important and tells the whole story.
9. Extended data Figure 1C – are IHx males resistant to changes in body weight at 17 days? Or is this driven by variability,
etc.?
10. Extended Figure 1C,D and elsewhere: Please clarify “age” on x-axis as number of days.
11. Results: line 169-170: the primary substrate in humans and in rodents for DNL is glucose, not other fatty acids (they do
indeed contribute but not to a great extent). Work has demonstrated this, in the brain, during development:
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-44388-4 (I see you cite this already later on as well – it should be mentioned
here for consistency).
12. Results: Line 180-182: “prolonged dysregulations in lipid homeostasis” – what kind of dysregulations?
Increased/decreased DNL? Increased/decreased oxidation? A bit of an oversimplified statement for your detailed results.
13. The concept of astrocytes being specialized to oxidize fatty acids is well-established (for example:
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gtc.13144) – is your finding novel in the timepoints/model selected? What makes
your finding novel?
14. Discussion is somewhat brief – more comparisons to the existing literature could be made on this topic.

### Reviewer 5

The manuscript by Fernandez et al. provides new evidence that during the critical period of brain development in neonates
born extremely prematurely, brain mitochondria increasingly rely on fatty acid oxidation. This metabolic shift coincides with a
reduction in total brain fatty acids and complex lipid classes, which may contribute to behavioral changes. The authors
demonstrate that supplementation with alternative fuels, such as acetate, in in vivo and in vitro models, spares fatty
acids and leads to improved neurological outcomes. Authors use of intermittent hypoxia as a model to study neonatal brain injury
in extremely preterm infants. Overall, the manuscript is well presented, and the major conclusions are supported by the data.
The reviewer suggests the following improvements to enhance the clarity and rigor of the manuscript:
1. Authors need to improve the consistency in Definitions of Fatty Acid Classes. In line 355, the authors consider very long-
chain fatty acids (VLCFA) as lipids with more than 22 carbons; however, in Figures 1J/K (and similarly in Extended Figures
2C/D, 9B/C), the cutoff appears to be 20 carbons. Can the authors reconcile this discrepancy between the results and
conclusions? For consistency, it is generally accepted that long-chain fatty acids (LCFA) include lipids with 12–20 carbons,
while VLCFA are those with 22–38 carbons. Distinguishing between these two categories is important, as the data treat all
fatty acids similarly, yet the discussion focuses primarily on VLCFA.
2. Presentation of Lipid Remodeling Data could be also improved. The changes shown in lipid remodeling of free fatty acids
appear modest (Figures 1I, Extended Figures 2B, 4F, 5D, 3C, and 9A), and the graphs make it difficult to discern statistically
significant trends. Rather than displaying all data, including non-significant changes, the authors could provide a
comprehensive table summarizing all results and only depict statistically significant changes in the figures for clarity.
3. Could the observed phenotype be explained simply by low body weight and, consequently, a reduced capacity to
accumulate adipose tissue, which is essential for normal brain development? The authors are encouraged to address this
possibility.
4. The authors report that supplementation with glycerol-triacetate improves neurological recovery based on NOR scores.
Does this treatment also result in improvements in brain lipidomic profiles, particularly in the hippocampus? Including this
data and more presenting more phenotypic data would strengthen the conclusions.
Minor Suggestions:
- The term “differentially expressed lipids” is somewhat misleading. Lipids, unlike genes, may not “express” information or
functions in the traditional sense; many serve structural roles, such as membrane components. The authors are encouraged
to clarify or replace this terminology.
- Extended Figure 1C-D: It would be valuable to include pre-intervention data as a control to confirm that both groups started
with comparable body weights.
- Extended Figure 4: The data likely represent fed-state levels; the authors should clarify this in the figure caption.

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
General comments:
In this study, Fernandez et al. investigated the impact of brain intermittent hypoxemia during
neonatal stage on lipid metabolism. Using a mouse model of neonatal brain injury due to
intermittent hypoxemia, the authors reported that it led to cognitive impairments later in life. They
also demonstrated that post-natal intermittent hypoxemia led to an alteration of lipid
profile signatured mainly by decreased levels of very long-chain fatty acids, which was associated with
enhanced mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation. The authors also demonstrated that acetate
treatment can promote functional recovery by sparing fatty acid oxidation.
The topic of investigation is novel and of high significance, the authors also performed a
comprehensive study with logical design, which led to conclusions that could potentially be of
clinical relevance. There are several considerations necessary to solidify their central conclusions,
including verification of findings in human samples, justification of model used, discussion of
potential sex differences, and interpretation of mechanism related to the altered lipid metabolism.
Major comments:
1. The study has been performed in a mouse IHx model. Although the study timeline was well-
designed, whether this model closely resembles EPT neonatal hypoxia-induced brain injury
demands further justification.
a) There are studies (e.g., PMID 33984336) reported that the age point as well as the interval of
hypoxia treatment regimen can lead to either impaired or improved memory function, the authors
should provide literature support regarding the basis of IHx model set up in this study.
Based on numerous clinical and preclinical studies, intermittent hypoxia due to apnea of
prematurity is detrimental to neurodevelopmental outcomes (PMID: 26262797, PMID: 15329741,
PMID: 25476492, and PMID: 28388601)1–4. Hyperoxia also has been found to be detrimental and
therefore, in the current clinical practice, titration of oxygen in extremely preterm infants is
common. In these patients, hyperoxia has been shown to contribute to other morbidities such as
retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), therefore currently, clinical practice aims to limit hyperoxia
(PMID: 31487704 and PMID: 20689332)5,6.
In the review paper that the reviewer cites (PMID: 33984336)7, intermittent hypoxia was used to
counterbalance hyperoxia and hyperoxia detrimental pathways. This review cites the works of
Bavis et al. (2019) (PMID 30439529)8 which explored carotid body development and brain stem
hypoxia ventilator response in a hyperoxia model during the first 12 days of postnatal
development. This paper (PMID 30439529)8 found that IHx improves carotid body development
but did not explore brain development. The other cited paper in this review article from Martin et
al. (2010)9 used a model of neonatal asphyxia with a single 5-min exposure to 100% N 24 hours
2
after birth followed by oxygen resuscitation. These two papers model different clinical paradigms
which are not related to apnea of prematurity. Our model of intermittent hypoxia recapitulates
apnea of prematurity which is characterized by multiple daily brief episodes of hypoxia with a rapid
return to normoxia (PMID: 33597229 and PMID: 33712716)10,11. This in clinical patients can
continue until age equivalent term.
The papers from Zhang et al. (2005)12 titled “Neonatal exposure to intermittent hypoxia enhances
mice performance in water maze and 8-arm radial maze tasks” and Zhang et al. (2014) (PMID:
24368168)13 sought to understand high altitude (2km) associated hypoxia effects on brain
development. Their intermittent hypoxia model consists of one 4-hr long exposure to 16% O daily
2
and does not represent brief repetitive episodes common to apnea of prematurity. Our study, in
contrast, aimed to understand the effects of multiple and brief episodes of hypoxia which last 20
seconds or longer and associated with low oxygen saturations. As clinicians (Susanna Scafidi,
MD – a pediatric ICU physician and Joseph Scafidi, DO – a neonatal neurologist and
neurodevelopmental specialist), we care for children born extremely preterm that experienced
apnea of prematurity and subsequent co-morbidities. Therefore, we utilized a model that mimics
our clinical experience and experience of other clinician scientists that are trying to address the
sequela of intermittent hypoxemia due to extremely preterm birth. Specifically, Vadim Ten, MD
(neonatologist) research group has shown that this model reflects neurologic, histologic, and
pathophysiologic changes observed in humans born extremely preterm (PMID: 25476492)3.
Other scientists such as Dr. Alexander Drobyshevsky’s research group also utilizes a similar
model of intermittent hypoxia to study the cellular effect on brain development (PMID: 39890465
and PMID: 30858028)14,15.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Summary
Fernandez et al. extensively addressed an existing gap in the literature surrounding changes in
brain lipid metabolism and the brain lipid profile in infants born extremely preterm (i.e. less than
28 weeks gestation following brain injury). Authors used an established model of neonatal brain
injury by subjecting mice to intermittent hypoxia (IHx) via episodes of hypoxia (32 cycles) from
P0-P11, alongside an arm of normoxia (Nx) controls. Male, and female pups from different litters
were used for the majority of experimentation at P11, P17, P22 and P30.
Authors examined the mouse hippocampus following injury and found that there was no change
between IHx and Nx groups in total hippocampal lipids, however, changes in lipid composition
were found that were in-part, sex-specific. Namely, at P30, males had significantly lower
hippocampal omega 9 fatty acids (n-9), while palmitic acid (16:0; PAM) and arachidonic acid
(20:4n-6; ARA) were significantly increased in IHx compared to Nx. In both sexes, very long chain
fatty acids (VLCFA; > or equal to 20 carbons) were significantly decreased in IHx compared to
Nx. Interestingly, PAM, the primary product of DNL was the top differentially expressed fatty acid
(FA) between IHx and Nx groups in males at P30.
Based on changes in hippocampal lipid composition, authors sought to rule out if these changes
were a result of altered nutrient supply following hypoxic injury. After measuring hippocampal
glucose uptake, circulating NEFA levels, plasma ketones and acyl-carnitines, and hippocampal
acyl-carnitines, it was concluded that the change in hippocampal lipid composition was not a result
of a limited supply of nutrients following injury. This led authors to conduct an unbiased
proteomics analysis of the hippocampus at P11, in order to identify proteins and pathways responsible for the
altered lipid composition following IHx. Postnatal day 11 was selected for proteomics because at
this timepoint, plasma levels of ketones and acyl-carnitines were increased in IHx compared to
Nx groups, and this corresponded to increased hippocampal acyl-carnitines – giving insight to
FAs being mobilized for the generation of acetyl-coA.
At P11, pathway analysis of proteomics data revealed the downregulation of multiple pathways
involved in the metabolism of lipids in the IHx group; specifically, the downregulation of genes
involved in FA oxidation (cpt2), the synthesis of long chain FA and cholesterol (scd2), lipid
regulators (acc1), and FASN. However, these changes were transient and recovered by P30 (for
example, FASN was downregulated at P11, and became upregulated by P30).
Authors then sought to address functional changes resulting from alterations in hippocampal lipid
composition by assessing the dependency of the hippocampus on different metabolic fuels. Using
a seahorse mito fuel flex test kit; validated by measuring the oxidation of substrates labelled with
14C, authors found that metabolic brain fuels utilized depend on time. Specifically, the injured
brain depends more on the oxidation of glucose at P11 only, while FA oxidation was high at P11,
and 6 days post injury (P17).
Because the hippocampal oxidation of FA remained high post-injury at P17, authors sought to
determine if the brain also had an increase in circulating FA uptake. Using an analogue of PAM
that cannot be metabolized (3H-2-bromopalmitate), authors found a significant increase in FA
uptake in IHx mice compared to Nx, alongside unchanged 14C-glutamine, -BHB and -lactate
uptakes at P17 between IHx and Nx. Authors concluded based on this result, that following
hypoxia, from P11 to recovery (P17), the brain upregulates FA oxidation to fuel and support
oxidative metabolism.
Since FA were extensively oxidized up until P17, authors then sought to measure the FA profile
of the hippocampus at P17. In both sexes, n-9 and total saturated fatty acids (SFAs) (> 20 carbons
– which accumulate during development and are extensively synthesized) were significantly lower
in IHx compared to Nx groups. Authors further characterized these changes in situ using non
targeted MS imaging in multiple brain regions, as well as in a conditional KO mouse of CPT2.
Together, these experiments showed IHx results in hippocampal region-specific lipid changes
(corroborating the total lipid fatty acid profile at P17), and astrocytes are the primary brain cells
that oxidize FAs.
Lastly, and arguably most importantly, authors tested acetate treatment in a) the media and b) in
vivo to investigate if acetate supply would spare FA from oxidation (using oleic acid; 18:1n-9;
OLA). Authors found treating the media with glucose to spare FA from oxidation did not impact
OLA oxidation, however, OLA oxidation in the presence of acetate decreased by 86% and 93%
at P11, and P17, respectively, in IHx compared to Nx. Next, authors found in-vivo acetate
treatment (glycerol-triacetate to pups by oral gavage; 5mg/g birth weight) daily from P11-P17
reduced 14C-OLA oxidation by 71% at P17 compared to glycerol (vehicle) in the IHx group.
Authors found in-vivo treatment with acetate also resulted in improved recognition indexes in the
Novel Object Recognition (NOR) test performed at the later timepoint of P30; suggesting an
improvement in recognition memory in addition to sparing FA from oxidation.
Altogether, Fernandez et al. employed exhaustive approaches to investigate and characterize
alterations following injury in the developing brain. As beta-oxidation is usually negligible in the
developing brain, this data provides novel evidence that is not the case following neonatal injury,
where beta-oxidation is significantly upregulated. This metabolic shift results in a decreased
VLCFA content in the brain, and interestingly, impacts cognitive performance (at P30) – in which
sparing FA from oxidation can improve neurologic outcomes (the opposite to what is observed in
adulthood, in which increased oxidation is associated with improved cognitive performance).
Importantly, this paper demonstrates the unique specificity of the injured brain with regards to
substrates utilized for oxidative metabolism during development, and results are promising for
beginning to investigate effective treatments following neonatal brain injury.
Specific comments:
Major comments:
1. Palmitic acid is the primary product of de novo lipogenesis (DNL) and happens to be identified
in males at P30 as the top differentially expressed FA in your volcano plot (Fig 1H; p < 0.001)
between IHx and Nx groups, which is consistent with IHx males having a significantly higher
hippocampal PAM at P30 than Nx males. Could DNL be increasing in your IHx group in
attempt to maintain brain energy requirements and/or FA balance in PL in response to injury?
Especially since FASN (the major governor of DNL) was also upregulated at P30 in IHx males?
Not a lot of discussion/hypotheses around this result, which also appears to be sex-specific.
We thank the reviewer for this comment and agree that increase in palmitic acid and de novo
lipogenesis can be an endogenous attempt to recover. Our data on hippocampal de novo
lipogenesis using acetate incorporation into lipids (Supplementary Figure 1) show no differences
between Nx and IHx at all ages. We chose this assay because it quantifies acetate incorporation
in both fatty acids and cholesterol while measured levels of palmitic acid reflect de novo
lipogenesis from glucose as demonstrated by Smith et al. (2024) (PMID: 38233416)35.
This current revised manuscript now includes P22 total lipid fatty acid data, which also shows an
increase in palmitic acid after IHx (albeit only in males). This age (P22) was evaluated because
mice are weaned at P21 and transition to a primarily carbohydrate rich rodent chow diet. These

The observed sex differences in brain lipid composition corroborate the results from the study by
Rodriguez-Navas et al. (2016) (PMID: 27656405)36 who showed sexual dimorphism in brain lipids
of adult mice fed a low and high fat diet. Further studies focused on sex differences at different
ages are needed since there exists several possibilities that could explain these observation.
Rodriguez-Navas et al. (2016) suggested that the sex differences may be explained by
differences in fatty acid uptake into the brain and expression of enzymes involved in fatty acid
metabolism, slower turnover of fatty acids, and possibly hormonal changes since they performed
studies using adult mice. Sexual dimorphism in mitochondrial respiration and oxidative stress has
been reported in other models of neonatal brain injury (PMID: 27197831)37. Together with our
results, these data suggest that sex differences in brain metabolism and lipid composition are
observed prior to major changes in hormones associated with growth and maturation. These
points are now included in our discussion section.

The hippocampus was selected because it is important for learning and memory formation.
Importantly, school aged children born extremely preterm display decreased hippocampal volume
as well as cognitive deficits, specifically – learning and memory. We now expanded on the rational
for selecting the hippocampus in the introduction and discussion and we mentioned in the
methods that this brain region was selected a priori.
Based on the MALDI-MSI imaging data at P17, we expect to have changes in other brain regions.
Current and future studies aim to delineate changes in other regions (white matter, cerebellum,
and cortex).

(% of total lipids per mg of tissue). Rather, it is lipid composition which changed. Language needs
to be 1) altered to reflect this is not a real “reduction”, and 2) clarify this result is region-specific.
We agree with the reviewer and changes in the language were made. Specifically, in the abstract

4. Presenting hippocampal lipid composition data in a supplemental table – as both concentration

The reviewer highlights an important request to provide access to the lipidomic data. We agree

values, to the supplementary information (Supplementary Tables 1,4,12, and 13) and source data
as tables. We will also post the data to a publicly accessible database.
The reviewer mentions the supplemental data should include concentrations. We would like to
clarify and more specifically describe how the lipid data was acquired and why the lipid data is
not reported as concentrations. The lipidomic data presented herein was acquired using a high-
throughput, targeted lipid profiling method. We have published previously using this methodology
(e.g., PMID: 39128713, 38986724, 38057386)38–40. The data was acquired using a standard and
accepted lipidomic method whereby lipid abundances were normalized to sum composition,
mean-centered, and log-transformed. The data as presented does not represent concentration
but rather abundance. This allows for visualizing hundreds of detected lipids with multivariate and
univariate statistical analyses. In addition, the data was acquired using spiked-in internal
standards (Avanti Polar Lipids EquiSplash #330731) which provided one deuterium stable-
labeled lipid per lipid class. The lipid standards allow for compensation during lipid extraction,
ionization efficiency, and provide a means for determining relative abundance.
5. There is an overall lack of justification surrounding why the hippocampus was selected for

synthesis? This could be explained better.
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. As mentioned above (comment #2) we selected the
hippocampus because of its role in learning and memory and susceptibility to injury in children
born extremely preterm term. The additional benefit of focusing of the hippocampus is that it
allows us to test function such as recognition memory and determine whether treatment (i.e.
glycerol-triacetate) will improve the memory deficits.
The hippocampus is a highly energetically demanding region of the brain. We previously showed
that the hippocampus displays a high expression of the carnitine shuttle – required for long-chain
fatty acid oxidation - compared to cortex and midbrain and has a high capacity to oxidize fatty
acids (PMID: 28512781)41. We expanded our discussion to highlight these features.
6. Pups were removed from the dam for extended periods of time very early in development to
undergo cycles of hypoxia (16 x 3 min hypoxia + 5 min re-oxygenation x 2 = 32 cycles). This is a
significant amount of time, and enough to impact maternal stress. Did authors measure and/or
consider maternal stress, and if this can program pups postnatally?
We did not consider maternal stress given that normoxia and intermittent hypoxia pups were
treated the same way. Both groups were separated from the mom for 16 cycles, return with the
dam for 2 hours in the home cage, and separated again for the remaining 16 cycles. Normoxia
pups were kept in a separate chamber under normal oxygen levels for the 2x 16 cycles. We did
not observe malnutrition (for example, plasma carnitine levels) or maternal neglect in either of the
groups.
Many models of neonatal brain injury require pups to be separated from the dam for a period of
time (ex: Hypoxia-Ischemia model) that can be as long as 90 minutes along with surgical
manipulations. In our model, there is limited handling of the dam therefore limiting stress.

which pups underwent which assay would aid in the reader understanding the results better.
Furthermore, the use of “mice” throughout the methods should specify the age, and sex of the

We thank the reviewer for the comment, and we would like to clarify that, due to a very small
tissue amounts, we used a new set of mice for every experiment presented in this manuscript (i.e.
FAO, acylcarnitines, lipidomics, total lipid fatty acids, MALDI, proteomics, RNA, etc.) All figure
legends report number of animals and sex used for each particular experiment. In addition, we
provided the exact number of mice used for each experiment as well as their age and sex in the

the brain. Perhaps there is between-tissue FA exchange to maintain total brain FAs.
Since the brain is essentially dependent on continuous blood supply of substrates and precursors,
we extensively measured the blood levels of glucose, lactate, βHB, NEFA, and acylcarnitines.
Recent data from Smith et al. (2024) (PMID: 38233416)35 showed that while peripheral tissues
(liver) undergo remodeling, brain levels were maintained. In our data, NEFA were changed only
at P22 – one day post-weaning from the dam. Plasma βHB levels were higher after IHx only at
P11 and P17. This increased in βHB suggests that hepatic ketogenesis was upregulated up to
P17. While peripheral tissue reprogramming after IHx would be an interesting focus for a future
study, in this work, we aimed to delineate metabolic reprogramming in the hippocampus after IHx.
9. IHx group weighs significantly less than Nx at most timepoints in both sexes. I understand this

metabolism, and substrates used for energy. Are hippocampal lipid alterations a result of hypoxia,

Thank you for your thoughtful comment. As this reviewer pointed out, we observed reduced body
weight gain in the IHx group up to P30 in both sexes. As mentioned above (comment #8), the
blood levels of substrates were maintained (glucose, lactate) or even increased (βHB) indicating
that delivery of substrates for brain energy and metabolism was comparable to Nx controls.
Therefore, these results suggest that hippocampal lipid alterations were not due to a limited
supply of substrates for brain energy and growth.
While substrate delivery was comparable to Nx, the fate of the substrates differ in the IHx group.
In this study, using biochemical and genetic approaches, we demonstrated that following IHx,
astrocytes extensively oxidized long-chain fatty acids – a process that is dismal in the developing
brain – and affected subsequent hippocampal lipid composition.

In a separate manuscript that is currently under review, we determined that triacetate treatment

(P11 and P17 but not P22). We appreciate the reviewer’s comment and we removed the word

4. Introduction: line 147: “clinically feasible source of acetate” – provide more detail supporting
why this is clinically feasible? I assume it has a bitter taste; it is recognized safe as a food additive
but what dose would it need to be administered as, and would this be GRAS?
Thank you for this comment. We would like to further clarify that the US Food and Drug
Administration (FDA) classifies glycerol-triacetate as GRAS (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-
21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-184/subpart-B/section-184.1901).
Clinically and in in vivo animal models, acetate cannot be administered on its own; it has to be
delivered as either sodium or potassium acetate and is usually administered intravenously in
humans. The concern is that in very vulnerable extremely preterm infants, the sodium or
potassium may cause a significant metabolic and electrolyte disturbance. Glycerol-triacetate
allows oral administration, is readily absorbed in the gut, and is an FDA compound not associated
with toxicity.
In our study, glycerol-triacetin (Millipore Sigma; 1030001000) was administered via gavage to
ensure that the full dose was given. At the dose that we administered (5mg/g body weight) we did
not see side effects. In order to determine the dose in humans, an IRB approved clinical trial
would be necessary. To bypass the bitter taste that can be associated with glycerol-triacetate,
the compound can be administered by oral gavage, which is often done in the neonatal intensive care
units (NICU).
In a study of two patients with Canavan disease, administration of glycerol-triacetate at 4.5g/kg
was well tolerated (PMID: 21474353)43.
