### Reviewer 3

Summary
Fernandez et al. extensively addressed an existing gap in the literature surrounding changes in brain lipid metabolism and
the brain lipid profile in infants born extremely preterm (i.e. less than 28 weeks gestation following brain injury). Authors used
an established model of neonatal brain injury by subjecting mice to intermittent hypoxia (IHx) via episodes of hypoxia (32
cycles) from P0-P11, alongside an arm of normoxia (Nx) controls. Male, and female pups from different litters
were used for the majority of experimentation at P11, P17, P22 and P30.
Authors examined the mouse hippocampus following injury and found that there was no change between IHx and Nx groups
in total hippocampal lipids, however, changes in lipid composition were found that were in-part, sex-specific. Namely, at
P30, males had significantly lower hippocampal omega 9 fatty acids (n-9), while palmitic acid (16:0; PAM) and arachidonic
acid (20:4n-6; ARA) were significantly increased in IHx compared to Nx. In both sexes, very long chain fatty acids (VLCFA; >
or equal to 20 carbons) were significantly decreased in IHx compared to Nx. Interestingly, PAM, the primary product of DNL
was the top differentially expressed fatty acid (FA) between IHx and Nx groups in males at P30.
Based on changes in hippocampal lipid composition, authors sought to rule out if these changes were a result of altered
nutrient supply following hypoxic injury. After measuring hippocampal glucose uptake, circulating NEFA levels, plasma
ketones and acyl-carnitines, and hippocampal acyl-carnitines, it was concluded that the change in hippocampal lipid
composition was not a result of a limited supply of nutrients following injury. This led authors to conduct an unbiased
proteomics analysis of the hippocampus at P11, in order to identify proteins and pathways responsible for the altered lipid
composition following IHx. Postnatal day 11 was selected for proteomics because at this timepoint, plasma levels of ketones
and acyl-carnitines were increased in IHx compared to Nx groups, and this corresponded to increased hippocampal acyl-
carnitines – giving insight to FAs being mobilized for the generation of acetyl-coA.
At P11, pathway analysis of proteomics data revealed the downregulation of multiple pathways involved in the metabolism
of lipids in the IHx group; specifically, the downregulation of genes involved in FA oxidation (cpt2), the synthesis of long
chain FA and cholesterol (scd2), lipid regulators (acc1), and FASN. However, these changes were transient and recovered
by P30 (for example, FASN was downregulated at P11, and became upregulated by P30).
Authors then sought to address functional changes resulting from alterations in hippocampal lipid composition by assessing
the dependency of the hippocampus on different metabolic fuels. Using a seahorse mito fuel flex test kit; validated by
measuring the oxidation of substrates labelled with 14C, authors found that metabolic brain fuels utilized depend on time.
Specifically, the injured brain depends more on the oxidation of glucose at P11 only, while FA oxidation was high at P11,
and 6 days post injury (P17).
Because the hippocampal oxidation of FA remained high post-injury at P17, authors sought to determine if the brain also
had an increase in circulating FA uptake. Using an analogue of PAM that cannot be metabolized (3H-2-bromopalmitate),
authors found a significant increase in FA uptake in IHx mice compared to Nx, alongside unchanged 14C-glutamine, -BHB
and -lactate uptakes at P17 between IHx and Nx. Authors concluded based on this result, that following
hypoxia, from P11 to recovery (P17), the brain upregulates FA oxidation to fuel and support
oxidative metabolism.
Since FA were extensively oxidized up until P17, authors then sought to measure the FA profile of the hippocampus at P17.
In both sexes, n-9 and total saturated fatty acids (SFAs) (> 20 carbons – which accumulate during development and are
extensively synthesized) were significantly lower in IHx compared to Nx groups. Authors further characterized these
changes in situ using non targeted MS imaging in multiple brain regions, as well as in a conditional KO mouse of CPT2.
Together, these experiments showed IHx results in hippocampal region-specific lipid changes
(corroborating the total lipid fatty acid profile at P17), and astrocytes are the primary brain cells
that oxidize FAs.
Lastly, and arguably most importantly, authors tested acetate treatment in a) the media and b) in vivo to investigate if acetate
supply would spare FA from oxidation (using oleic acid; 18:1n-9; OLA). Authors found treating the media with glucose to
spare FA from oxidation did not impact OLA oxidation, however, OLA oxidation in the presence of acetate decreased by
86% and 93% at P11, and P17, respectively, in IHx compared to Nx. Next, authors found in-vivo acetate treatment (glycerol-
triacetate to pups by oral gavage; 5mg/g birth weight) daily from P11-P17 reduced 14C-OLA oxidation by 71% at P17
compared to glycerol (vehicle) in the IHx group. Authors found in-vivo treatment with acetate also resulted in improved
recognition indexes in the Novel Object Recognition (NOR) test performed at the later timepoint of P30; suggesting an
improvement in recognition memory in addition to sparing FA from oxidation.
Altogether, Fernandez et al. employed exhaustive approaches to investigate and characterize
alterations following injury in the developing brain. As beta-oxidation is usually negligible in the developing brain, this data provides novel evidence that
is not the case following neonatal injury, where beta-oxidation is significantly upregulated. This metabolic shift results in a
decreased VLCFA content in the brain, and interestingly, impacts cognitive performance (at P30) – in which
sparing FA from oxidation can improve neurologic outcomes (the opposite to what is observed in
adulthood, in which increased oxidation is associated with improved cognitive performance).
Importantly, this paper demonstrates the unique specificity of the injured brain with regards to
substrates utilized for oxidative metabolism during development, and results are promising for
beginning to investigate effective treatments following neonatal brain injury.
Specific comments:
Major comments:
1. Palmitic acid is the primary product of de novo lipogenesis (DNL) and happens to be identified in males at P30 as the top
differentially expressed FA in your volcano plot (Fig 1H; p < 0.001) between IHx and Nx groups, which is consistent with IHx
males having a significantly higher hippocampal PAM at P30 than Nx males. Could DNL be increasing in your IHx group in
attempt to maintain brain energy requirements and/or FA balance in PL in response to injury? Especially since FASN (the
major governor of DNL) was also upregulated at P30 in IHx males? Not a lot of discussion/hypotheses around this result,
which also appears to be sex-specific.
2. Almost all results shown are limited to the hippocampus, and not the whole brain (other than the MS imaging data). How
might you predict your findings to change at the level of the whole brain, or other regions? If hippocampus was important a
priori this could be mentioned.
3. Authors state there is a “reduction” in brain lipids in the abstract and elsewhere, however, total lipids in the hippocampus
(primary region examined) are unchanged between IHx and Nx groups (% of total lipids per mg of tissue). Rather, it is lipid
composition which changed. Language needs to be 1) altered to reflect this is not a real “reduction”, and 2) clarify this result
is region-specific.
4. Presenting hippocampal lipid composition data in a supplemental table – as both concentration and relative %,
would be useful to the reader.
5. There is an overall lack of justification surrounding why the hippocampus was selected for analyses (see comment
above), besides the obvious reason it corresponds to behavioural analyses conducted. Is the hippocampus equipped for
oxidation compared to others? Lipid synthesis? This could be explained better.
6. Pups were removed from the dam for extended periods of time very early in development to undergo cycles of hypoxia (16
x 3 min hypoxia + 5 min re-oxygenation x 2 = 32 cycles). This is a significant amount of time, and enough to impact maternal
stress. Did authors measure and/or consider maternal stress, and if this can program pups postnatally?
7. This is a lot of assays for a very small brain tissue to undergo. A supplemental table outlining which pups underwent
which assay would aid in the reader understanding the results better. Furthermore, the use of “mice” throughout the methods
should specify the age, and sex of the mice as authors used many timepoints and both sexes.
8. Were any other tissues collected from these mice? It would be nice to see the FA composition of a peripheral tissue like
the liver and rule out if total lipids changed in peripheral tissues, but not the brain. Perhaps there is between-tissue FA
exchange to maintain total brain FAs.
9. IHx group weighs significantly less than Nx at most timepoints in both sexes. I understand this is necessary to model
extremely preterm infants, however, this could also impact overall metabolism, and substrates used for energy. Are
hippocampal lipid alterations a result of hypoxia, weight loss, or both?
Minor comments:
1. Abstract: The abstract overall is a bit boilerplate for the results described. Adding more detail to the results with regards to
timepoints, sex, etc. would better capture your findings.
2. Abstract: Line 109: “timely” supply – again, we know this is a critical period of brain development but what exactly are the
timepoints that the intervention (triacetin) would have the most benefit?
3. Introduction: line 143: provide a citation for IHx as clinically relevant model of neonatal brain injury?
4. Introduction: line 147: “clinically feasible source of acetate” – provide more detail supporting why this is clinically feasible?
I assume it has a bitter taste; it is recognized safe as a food additive but what dose would it need to be administered as, and
would this be GRAS?
5. Language around timepoints selected and interpretation:
a. Line 153-154: the “neonatal period” authors selected not only impacts what would be a premature infant (PND 1-2/3 in a
mouse), but also the window of a term infant (PND 7-10 mouse) – translationally, are children that are born extremely
preterm exposed to intermittent hypoxia as a term infant, as well?
b. By P30 in a mouse, the brain is 90-95% of adult weight and corresponds to what would be a 2-3 year old child. Be careful
with language around this timepoint referring to “later” in life.
6. Figure 1B-D and Extended Figure 1A-B: Add units for x-axis (i.e. “day 30” or “P30”). It is unclear what units you are
referring to.
7. Figure 1E-F: Inconsistency in naming of PC 1/2 – pick either PC or component.
8. I would consider adding the differentially expressed fatty acid data for females into the figure with males, as it is equally as
important and tells the whole story.
9. Extended data Figure 1C – are IHx males resistant to changes in body weight at 17 days? Or is this driven by variability,
etc.?
10. Extended Figure 1C,D and elsewhere: Please clarify “age” on x-axis as number of days.
11. Results: line 169-170: the primary substrate in humans and in rodents for DNL is glucose, not other fatty acids (they do
indeed contribute but not to a great extent). Work has demonstrated this, in the brain, during development:
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-44388-4 (I see you cite this already later on as well – it should be mentioned
here for consistency).
12. Results: Line 180-182: “prolonged dysregulations in lipid homeostasis” – what kind of dysregulations?
Increased/decreased DNL? Increased/decreased oxidation? A bit of an oversimplified statement for your detailed results.
13. The concept of astrocytes being specialized to oxidize fatty acids is well-established (for example:
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/gtc.13144) – is your finding novel in the timepoints/model selected? What makes
your finding novel?
14. Discussion is somewhat brief – more comparisons to the existing literature could be made on this topic.
15. What kind of diets were the pups on post-weaning, or the dams throughout the study? This is not mentioned in the
manuscript.
16. Were the mice bred in-house, or were the dams ordered pregnant? This is not clear.
17. What methods were used for randomization? (line 405, line 419)
18. Who conducted the behavioural tests, as well as most analyses? Were investigators blinded or unblinded to treatment?
19. Clarify what portion of the brain was used for lipidomics (line 516) – was this from the same brains that the hippocampus
was taken from? Left vs. right hemisphere? Remaining whole brain?
20. Sample size is listed as a range in figure legends (ex. 7-13/sex/group/treatment) – as per Nature Comm requirements,
sample size must specify the total number of mice per sex, per treatment and not be presented in a range format.
21. Sample size for NOR test is rather small, is this enough power to detect changes?
22. Were the RT PCR data validated?
23. Authors refer to VLCFA as FA > 20 carbons – is it 20 or 22 that deems them VLCFA? Check IUPAC
24. Lines 187-189, you state the developing brain uses fatty acids for brain lipid synthesis, then follow it with the developing
brain extensively using glucose for de novo synthesis of fatty acids – these statements contradict each other.
25. As per Nature Comm requirements “as previously described” must be replaced with exactly how the procedure was
carried out (line 661) in the methods sections
26. Blood measurements in pups – these were unfasted or fasted?

### Reviewer 5

The manuscript by Fernandez et al. provides new evidence that during the critical period of brain development in neonates
born extremely prematurely, brain mitochondria increasingly rely on fatty acid oxidation. This metabolic shift coincides with a
reduction in total brain fatty acids and complex lipid classes, which may contribute to behavioral changes. The authors
demonstrate that supplementation with alternative fuels, such as acetate, in in vivo and in vitro models, spares fatty
acids and leads to improved neurological outcomes. Authors use of intermittent hypoxia as a model to study neonatal brain injury
in extremely preterm infants. Overall, the manuscript is well presented, and the major conclusions are supported by the data.
The reviewer suggests the following improvements to enhance the clarity and rigor of the manuscript:
1. Authors need to improve the consistency in Definitions of Fatty Acid Classes. In line 355, the authors consider very long-
chain fatty acids (VLCFA) as lipids with more than 22 carbons; however, in Figures 1J/K (and similarly in Extended Figures
2C/D, 9B/C), the cutoff appears to be 20 carbons. Can the authors reconcile this discrepancy between the results and
conclusions? For consistency, it is generally accepted that long-chain fatty acids (LCFA) include lipids with 12–20 carbons,
while VLCFA are those with 22–38 carbons. Distinguishing between these two categories is important, as the data treat all
fatty acids similarly, yet the discussion focuses primarily on VLCFA.
2. Presentation of Lipid Remodeling Data could be also improved. The changes shown in lipid remodeling of free fatty acids
appear modest (Figures 1I, Extended Figures 2B, 4F, 5D, 3C, and 9A), and the graphs make it difficult to discern statistically
significant trends. Rather than displaying all data, including non-significant changes, the authors could provide a
comprehensive table summarizing all results and only depict statistically significant changes in the figures for clarity.
3. Could the observed phenotype be explained simply by low body weight and, consequently, a reduced capacity to
accumulate adipose tissue, which is essential for normal brain development? The authors are encouraged to address this
possibility.
4. The authors report that supplementation with glycerol-triacetate improves neurological recovery based on NOR scores.
Does this treatment also result in improvements in brain lipidomic profiles, particularly in the hippocampus? Including this
data and more presenting more phenotypic data would strengthen the conclusions.
Minor Suggestions:
- The term “differentially expressed lipids” is somewhat misleading. Lipids, unlike genes, may not “express” information or
functions in the traditional sense; many serve structural roles, such as membrane components. The authors are encouraged
to clarify or replace this terminology.
- Extended Figure 1C-D: It would be valuable to include pre-intervention data as a control to confirm that both groups started
with comparable body weights.
- Extended Figure 4: The data likely represent fed-state levels; the authors should clarify this in the figure caption.

Based on numerous clinical and preclinical studies, intermittent hypoxia due to apnea of
prematurity is detrimental to neurodevelopmental outcomes (PMID: 26262797, PMID: 15329741,
PMID: 25476492, and PMID: 28388601)1–4. Hyperoxia also has been found to be detrimental and
therefore, in the current clinical practice, titration of oxygen in extremely preterm infants is
common. In these patients, hyperoxia has been shown to contribute to other morbidities such as
retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), therefore currently, clinical practice aims to limit hyperoxia
(PMID: 31487704 and PMID: 20689332)5,6.
In the review paper that the reviewer cites (PMID: 33984336)7, intermittent hypoxia was used to
counterbalance hyperoxia and hyperoxia detrimental pathways. This review cites the works of
Bavis et al. (2019) (PMID 30439529)8 which explored carotid body development and brain stem
hypoxia ventilator response in a hyperoxia model during the first 12 days of postnatal
development. This paper (PMID 30439529)8 found that IHx improves carotid body development
but did not explore brain development. The other cited paper in this review article from Martin et
al. (2010)9 used a model of neonatal asphyxia with a single 5-min exposure to 100% N 24 hours
2
after birth followed by oxygen resuscitation. These two papers model different clinical paradigms
which are not related to apnea of prematurity. Our model of intermittent hypoxia recapitulates
apnea of prematurity which is characterized by multiple daily brief episodes of hypoxia with a rapid
return to normoxia (PMID: 33597229 and PMID: 33712716)10,11. This in clinical patients can
continue until age equivalent term.
The papers from Zhang et al. (2005)12 titled “Neonatal exposure to intermittent hypoxia enhances
mice performance in water maze and 8-arm radial maze tasks” and Zhang et al. (2014) (PMID:
24368168)13 sought to understand high altitude (2km) associated hypoxia effects on brain
development. Their intermittent hypoxia model consists of one 4-hr long exposure to 16% O daily
2
and does not represent brief repetitive episodes common to apnea of prematurity. Our study, in
contrast, aimed to understand the effects of multiple and brief episodes of hypoxia which last 20
seconds or longer and associated with low oxygen saturations. As clinicians (Susanna Scafidi,
MD – a pediatric ICU physician and Joseph Scafidi, DO – a neonatal neurologist and
neurodevelopmental specialist), we care for children born extremely preterm that experienced
apnea of prematurity and subsequent co-morbidities. Therefore, we utilized a model that mimics
our clinical experience and experience of other clinician scientists that are trying to address the
sequela of intermittent hypoxemia due to extremely preterm birth. Specifically, Vadim Ten, MD
(neonatologist) research group has shown that this model reflects neurologic, histologic, and
pathophysiologic changes observed in humans born extremely preterm (PMID: 25476492)3.
Other scientists such as Dr. Alexander Drobyshevsky’s research group also utilizes a similar
model of intermittent hypoxia to study the cellular effect on brain development (PMID: 39890465
and PMID: 30858028)14,15.
b) Given the importance of time frame of IHx poses on the outcome, and the fact that IHx in human
infant started preterm (EPT birth), this model is using a full term born mouse model to mimic post
birth IHx, whether this could cause a difference in the lipid or protein profile needs to be
considered/discussed.
We agree with the reviewer that timing is critical during brain development. It has been established
that the rodent’s first 8-10 days (Postnatal days 0-10) of postnatal life have biological features
similar to human brains in the 3rd trimester of gestation. Numerous original research studies
delineate different aspects of brain development in humans and rodents. Below is a list of several
reviews that summarize the pertinent findings:
PMID: 2358330716
PMID: 1531333417
PMID: 3324657818
PMID: 3456937519
In fact, the emergence of new technology has enabled researchers to obtain more granular and
sophisticated data to correlate similar features between humans and other species such as
rodents. Newer generated data further confirms the choice of age in our model (PMID:
39870528)20.
In the revised version of the manuscript, we include citations that report “the sequence of key
events in brain maturation is largely consistent between humans and rodents” during development
(PMID: 23583307)16.
2. The authors have demonstrated astrocyte as the major source of the increased fatty acid
oxidation (FAO) after IHx using an astrocyte-specific CPT2 ko mouse model. This may align with
the fact that astrocytes are the main cell for lipid metabolism and function as a supporter for
neurons. However, myelination is also in high demand during post-natal stage, and myelin is well-
known to be highly-enriched in VLCFA. In Fig.1G, multiple top-altered lipid species are
cerebrosides (Hex1Cer, Hex2Cer) that are specifically abundant in myelin sheaths. The possibility
of potential contribution of oligodendrocytes to the altered lipid profile under IHx condition should
be re-evaluated and discussed.
We thank the reviewer for the insightful question. Altered sphingolipids are associated with
inflammation, autophagy, cell growth and survival (PMID: 26703189, PMID: 26943039, and
PMID: 22230369)21–23. In this study, the lipidomic profile was performed on microdissected
hippocampus, thus, several cell types can be affected (PMID: 32937123)24. Our lipidomic profile
has shown that at P30 (19 days post-IHx) several Hex1Cer and Hex2Cer species were both down-
and up-regulated (See table below). Indeed, oligodendrocytes, which contain high levels of
HexCer, can be affected in this model and we are currently exploring this further specifically in
microdissected subcortical white matter. As noted in the review “Lipid metabolism in astrocytic
structure and function” by Lee et al. (2021)25, changes to astrocyte sphingolipid structure and
metabolism have been described in various neurodegenerative diseases (PMID: 15590150,
PMID: 22810490, and PMID: 30803453)26–28. Specifically, astrocyte production of cerebrosides
(HexCer) as precursors to gangliosides supports healthy neurite outgrowth, regulates neuronal
inflammation, and stabilizes neuron-glia interactions (PMID: 31724708)29.
Recently, McInnis et al. (2024) (PMID: 39616264)30 reported that human iPSCs derived neurons
and glia respond differently to ceramides. Thus, the detection of altered sphingolipids during
development between Nx and IHx supports that sphingolipids play a pivotal role in cellular
physiology including development and after intermittent hypoxemia.

We thank the reviewer for pointing this fact out. Changes in gene and protein expression often
require assessment of function by measuring their activity and/or product/intermediate produced
by this particular protein. It is generally accepted that increased protein expression is associated
with increased function. However, existing proteins might carry out activity very efficiently even at
the small levels thus generating negative feedback loop which results in post-translational
changes, i.e. reduced transcription or increased degradation of mRNA. Similarly, decreased
activity may trigger increase in mRNA expression and subsequent protein increase. Several
recent studies, albeit in other tissues (liver, muscle), explored the discordance between the levels
of mRNA, protein, and activity (PMID: 40376090)33. Caution and thorough experimental
evaluation is underscored in a recent article by Lee et al. in Nature Metabolism (PMID:
40211046)34. Our approach in this study was to comprehensively assess gene and protein
expression as well as function (Seahorse, oxidation studies and quantification of metabolites).
As pointed out by the reviewer, we used [1-14C]-oleic acid to assess β-oxidation of fatty acids
since there is no [U-14C]-oleic acid available. Using [1-14C]-oleic acid, we are measuring the first
cycle, which contains the activation and transport steps involving the β-oxidations enzymes, which
is the rate-limiting cycle. We are measuring oxidation of the same fatty acid under different
conditions. In addition, we also included in the manuscript the acid soluble metabolites (ASMs)
(see Supplementary Figures 7 and 9). Our data demonstrates changes in CO production without
2
changes in ASMs. This signifies that β-oxidation of the fatty acid is near-complete.

2

11. The study in mouse model is comprehensive, yet the study lacks verification of its findings in
human samples/models. Considering the difficulty of acquiring human infant brain samples, some of
the findings from this study could potentially be verified using samples from brain tissues of
post-mortem infant who has experienced hypoxia (for example, hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy
infant cases are available from NIH NeuroBioBank). Also, some of the findings in blood samples
can be easily verified in human.
We do agree with this reviewer that our pursuit of a mouse study was to understand human
pathology. We appreciate that this reviewer understands the difficulties of obtaining human brain
tissue at school age. While blood samples might be easier to obtain, logistically it will require IRB,
patient recruitment, and specific biomarker analysis. As we demonstrate in this manuscript, many
processes occur specifically in the brain, and blood levels did not reflect brain changes in
circulating fatty acids, acylcarnitines, and other metabolites.
Diagnosis of hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy represents a different diagnosis and pathological
process. Specifically, newborns (both term and any gestational age pre-term) will sustain acute
single episode of asphyxia/hypoxia and subsequent ischemia often due to umbilical cord wrap
around the neck at the time of delivery or decrease in focal delivery. In term neonates, the extent
of immediate injury is determined clinically by the Sarnat scoring, however, this scoring does not
apply to preterm neonates. In contrast, nearly 100% of extremely preterm newborns have
numerous episodes of apnea of prematurity, associated with brief low oxygen levels and these
episodes continue during the entire time till infants reach corrected full-term age.
We did contact the NIH NeuroBioBank as per reviewer suggestion. There were no human
samples with history of prematurity at school age. We were able to get a small cohort of human
samples for both term (control) and extremely preterm (<28 weeks of gestation) infants. We
performed total lipid fatty acid analysis, which is now presented in Supplemental Figure 2. These
results are comparable to mouse brain tissue total lipid fatty acid profile at P11.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Summary
Fernandez et al. extensively addressed an existing gap in the literature surrounding changes in
brain lipid metabolism and the brain lipid profile in infants born extremely preterm (i.e. less than
28 weeks gestation following brain injury). Authors used an established model of neonatal brain
injury by subjecting mice to intermittent hypoxia (IHx) via episodes of hypoxia (32 cycles) from
P0-P11, alongside an arm of normoxia (Nx) controls. Male, and female pups from different litters
were used for the majority of experimentation at P11, P17, P22 and P30.
Authors examined the mouse hippocampus following injury and found that there was no change
between IHx and Nx groups in total hippocampal lipids, however, changes in lipid composition
were found that were in-part, sex-specific. Namely, at P30, males had significantly lower
hippocampal omega 9 fatty acids (n-9), while palmitic acid (16:0; PAM) and arachidonic acid
(20:4n-6; ARA) were significantly increased in IHx compared to Nx. In both sexes, very long chain
fatty acids (VLCFA; > or equal to 20 carbons) were significantly decreased in IHx compared to
Nx. Interestingly, PAM, the primary product of DNL was the top differentially expressed fatty acid
(FA) between IHx and Nx groups in males at P30.
Based on changes in hippocampal lipid composition, authors sought to rule out if these changes
were a result of altered nutrient supply following hypoxic injury. After measuring hippocampal
glucose uptake, circulating NEFA levels, plasma ketones and acyl-carnitines, and hippocampal
acyl-carnitines, it was concluded that the change in hippocampal lipid composition was not a result
of a limited supply of nutrients following injury. This led authors to conduct an unbiased
proteomics analysis of the hippocampus at P11, in order to identify proteins and pathways responsible for the
altered lipid composition following IHx. Postnatal day 11 was selected for proteomics because at
this timepoint, plasma levels of ketones and acyl-carnitines were increased in IHx compared to
Nx groups, and this corresponded to increased hippocampal acyl-carnitines – giving insight to
FAs being mobilized for the generation of acetyl-coA.
At P11, pathway analysis of proteomics data revealed the downregulation of multiple pathways
involved in the metabolism of lipids in the IHx group; specifically, the downregulation of genes
involved in FA oxidation (cpt2), the synthesis of long chain FA and cholesterol (scd2), lipid
regulators (acc1), and FASN. However, these changes were transient and recovered by P30 (for
example, FASN was downregulated at P11, and became upregulated by P30).
Authors then sought to address functional changes resulting from alterations in hippocampal lipid
composition by assessing the dependency of the hippocampus on different metabolic fuels. Using
a seahorse mito fuel flex test kit; validated by measuring the oxidation of substrates labelled with
14C, authors found that metabolic brain fuels utilized depend on time. Specifically, the injured
brain depends more on the oxidation of glucose at P11 only, while FA oxidation was high at P11,
and 6 days post injury (P17).
Because the hippocampal oxidation of FA remained high post-injury at P17, authors sought to
determine if the brain also had an increase in circulating FA uptake. Using an analogue of PAM
that cannot be metabolized (3H-2-bromopalmitate), authors found a significant increase in FA
uptake in IHx mice compared to Nx, alongside unchanged 14C-glutamine, -BHB and -lactate
uptakes at P17 between IHx and Nx. Authors concluded based on this result, that following
hypoxia, from P11 to recovery (P17), the brain upregulates FA oxidation to fuel and support
oxidative metabolism.
Since FA were extensively oxidized up until P17, authors then sought to measure the FA profile
of the hippocampus at P17. In both sexes, n-9 and total saturated fatty acids (SFAs) (> 20 carbons
– which accumulate during development and are extensively synthesized) were significantly lower
in IHx compared to Nx groups. Authors further characterized these changes in situ using non
targeted MS imaging in multiple brain regions, as well as in a conditional KO mouse of CPT2.
Together, these experiments showed IHx results in hippocampal region-specific lipid changes
(corroborating the total lipid fatty acid profile at P17), and astrocytes are the primary brain cells
that oxidize FAs.
Lastly, and arguably most importantly, authors tested acetate treatment in a) the media and b) in
vivo to investigate if acetate supply would spare FA from oxidation (using oleic acid; 18:1n-9;
OLA). Authors found treating the media with glucose to spare FA from oxidation did not impact
OLA oxidation, however, OLA oxidation in the presence of acetate decreased by 86% and 93%
at P11, and P17, respectively, in IHx compared to Nx. Next, authors found in-vivo acetate
treatment (glycerol-triacetate to pups by oral gavage; 5mg/g birth weight) daily from P11-P17
reduced 14C-OLA oxidation by 71% at P17 compared to glycerol (vehicle) in the IHx group.
Authors found in-vivo treatment with acetate also resulted in improved recognition indexes in the
Novel Object Recognition (NOR) test performed at the later timepoint of P30; suggesting an
improvement in recognition memory in addition to sparing FA from oxidation.
Altogether, Fernandez et al. employed exhaustive approaches to investigate and characterize
alterations following injury in the developing brain. As beta-oxidation is usually negligible in the
developing brain, this data provides novel evidence that is not the case following neonatal injury,
where beta-oxidation is significantly upregulated. This metabolic shift results in a decreased
VLCFA content in the brain, and interestingly, impacts cognitive performance (at P30) – in which
sparing FA from oxidation can improve neurologic outcomes (the opposite to what is observed in
adulthood, in which increased oxidation is associated with improved cognitive performance).
Importantly, this paper demonstrates the unique specificity of the injured brain with regards to
substrates utilized for oxidative metabolism during development, and results are promising for
beginning to investigate effective treatments following neonatal brain injury.
Specific comments:
Major comments:
1. Palmitic acid is the primary product of de novo lipogenesis (DNL) and happens to be identified
in males at P30 as the top differentially expressed FA in your volcano plot (Fig 1H; p < 0.001)
between IHx and Nx groups, which is consistent with IHx males having a significantly higher
hippocampal PAM at P30 than Nx males. Could DNL be increasing in your IHx group in
attempt to maintain brain energy requirements and/or FA balance in PL in response to injury?
Especially since FASN (the major governor of DNL) was also upregulated at P30 in IHx males?
Not a lot of discussion/hypotheses around this result, which also appears to be sex-specific.
We thank the reviewer for this comment and agree that increase in palmitic acid and de novo
lipogenesis can be an endogenous attempt to recover. Our data on hippocampal de novo
lipogenesis using acetate incorporation into lipids (Supplementary Figure 1) show no differences
between Nx and IHx at all ages. We chose this assay because it quantifies acetate incorporation
in both fatty acids and cholesterol while measured levels of palmitic acid reflect de novo
lipogenesis from glucose as demonstrated by Smith et al. (2024) (PMID: 38233416)35.
This current revised manuscript now includes P22 total lipid fatty acid data, which also shows an
increase in palmitic acid after IHx (albeit only in males). This age (P22) was evaluated because
mice are weaned at P21 and transition to a primarily carbohydrate rich rodent chow diet. These
results allowed us to delineate the trajectory of palmitic acid in the brain following IHx. In males,
immediately after IHx (P11), and during early recovery (P17), the levels of palmitic acid are
comparable to the levels observed in Nx hippocampus. However, at P22 and P30, the levels of
palmitic acid significantly increase in the IHx group hippocampus indicating increase de novo
lipogenesis. In contrast, females displayed palmitic acid levels equivalent to Nx hippocampus at
all ages. Taken together, these data suggests that the increase in hippocampal palmitic acid may
be related to the recovery process that the brain is undergoing.

The observed sex differences in brain lipid composition corroborate the results from the study by
Rodriguez-Navas et al. (2016) (PMID: 27656405)36 who showed sexual dimorphism in brain lipids
of adult mice fed a low and high fat diet. Further studies focused on sex differences at different
ages are needed since there exists several possibilities that could explain these observation.
Rodriguez-Navas et al. (2016) suggested that the sex differences may be explained by
differences in fatty acid uptake into the brain and expression of enzymes involved in fatty acid
metabolism, slower turnover of fatty acids, and possibly hormonal changes since they performed
studies using adult mice. Sexual dimorphism in mitochondrial respiration and oxidative stress has
been reported in other models of neonatal brain injury (PMID: 27197831)37. Together with our
results, these data suggest that sex differences in brain metabolism and lipid composition are
observed prior to major changes in hormones associated with growth and maturation. These
points are now included in our discussion section.
2. Almost all results shown are limited to the hippocampus, and not the whole brain (other than
the MS imaging data). How might you predict your findings to change at the level of the whole
brain, or other regions? If hippocampus was important a priori this could be mentioned.
The hippocampus was selected because it is important for learning and memory formation.
Importantly, school aged children born extremely preterm display decreased hippocampal volume
as well as cognitive deficits, specifically – learning and memory. We now expanded on the rational
for selecting the hippocampus in the introduction and discussion and we mentioned in the
methods that this brain region was selected a priori.
Based on the MALDI-MSI imaging data at P17, we expect to have changes in other brain regions.
Current and future studies aim to delineate changes in other regions (white matter, cerebellum,
and cortex).
3. Authors state there is a “reduction” in brain lipids in the abstract and elsewhere, however, total
lipids in the hippocampus (primary region examined) are unchanged between IHx and Nx groups
(% of total lipids per mg of tissue). Rather, it is lipid composition which changed. Language needs
to be 1) altered to reflect this is not a real “reduction”, and 2) clarify this result is region-specific.
We agree with the reviewer and changes in the language were made. Specifically, in the abstract
we changed “reduction in fatty acids” to “change in hippocampal fatty acid profile”.
4. Presenting hippocampal lipid composition data in a supplemental table – as both concentration
and relative %, would be useful to the reader.
The reviewer highlights an important request to provide access to the lipidomic data. We agree
the lipid data will be made available. We will add the lipid data, both abundances and normalized
values, to the supplementary information (Supplementary Tables 1,4,12, and 13) and source data
as tables. We will also post the data to a publicly accessible database.
The reviewer mentions the supplemental data should include concentrations. We would like to
clarify and more specifically describe how the lipid data was acquired and why the lipid data is
not reported as concentrations. The lipidomic data presented herein was acquired using a high-
throughput, targeted lipid profiling method. We have published previously using this methodology
(e.g., PMID: 39128713, 38986724, 38057386)38–40. The data was acquired using a standard and
accepted lipidomic method whereby lipid abundances were normalized to sum composition,
mean-centered, and log-transformed. The data as presented does not represent concentration
but rather abundance. This allows for visualizing hundreds of detected lipids with multivariate and
univariate statistical analyses. In addition, the data was acquired using spiked-in internal
standards (Avanti Polar Lipids EquiSplash #330731) which provided one deuterium stable-
labeled lipid per lipid class. The lipid standards allow for compensation during lipid extraction,
ionization efficiency, and provide a means for determining relative abundance.
5. There is an overall lack of justification surrounding why the hippocampus was selected for
analyses (see comment above), besides the obvious reason it corresponds to behavioral
analyses conducted. Is the hippocampus equipped for oxidation compared to others? Lipid
synthesis? This could be explained better.
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. As mentioned above (comment #2) we selected the
hippocampus because of its role in learning and memory and susceptibility to injury in children
born extremely preterm term. The additional benefit of focusing of the hippocampus is that it
allows us to test function such as recognition memory and determine whether treatment (i.e.
glycerol-triacetate) will improve the memory deficits.
The hippocampus is a highly energetically demanding region of the brain. We previously showed
that the hippocampus displays a high expression of the carnitine shuttle – required for long-chain
fatty acid oxidation - compared to cortex and midbrain and has a high capacity to oxidize fatty
acids (PMID: 28512781)41. We expanded our discussion to highlight these features.
6. Pups were removed from the dam for extended periods of time very early in development to
undergo cycles of hypoxia (16 x 3 min hypoxia + 5 min re-oxygenation x 2 = 32 cycles). This is a
significant amount of time, and enough to impact maternal stress. Did authors measure and/or
consider maternal stress, and if this can program pups postnatally?
We did not consider maternal stress given that normoxia and intermittent hypoxia pups were
treated the same way. Both groups were separated from the mom for 16 cycles, return with the
dam for 2 hours in the home cage, and separated again for the remaining 16 cycles. Normoxia
pups were kept in a separate chamber under normal oxygen levels for the 2x 16 cycles. We did
not observe malnutrition (for example, plasma carnitine levels) or maternal neglect in either of the
groups.
Many models of neonatal brain injury require pups to be separated from the dam for a period of
time (ex: Hypoxia-Ischemia model) that can be as long as 90 minutes along with surgical
manipulations. In our model, there is limited handling of the dam therefore limiting stress.

which pups underwent which assay would aid in the reader understanding the results better.
Furthermore, the use of “mice” throughout the methods should specify the age, and sex of the
mice as authors used many timepoints and both sexes.
We thank the reviewer for the comment, and we would like to clarify that, due to a very small
tissue amounts, we used a new set of mice for every experiment presented in this manuscript (i.e.
FAO, acylcarnitines, lipidomics, total lipid fatty acids, MALDI, proteomics, RNA, etc.) All figure
legends report number of animals and sex used for each particular experiment. In addition, we
provided the exact number of mice used for each experiment as well as their age and sex in the
source data file.
8. Were any other tissues collected from these mice? It would be nice to see the FA composition
of a peripheral tissue like the liver and rule out if total lipids changed in peripheral tissues, but not
the brain. Perhaps there is between-tissue FA exchange to maintain total brain FAs.
Since the brain is essentially dependent on continuous blood supply of substrates and precursors,
we extensively measured the blood levels of glucose, lactate, βHB, NEFA, and acylcarnitines.
Recent data from Smith et al. (2024) (PMID: 38233416)35 showed that while peripheral tissues
(liver) undergo remodeling, brain levels were maintained. In our data, NEFA were changed only
at P22 – one day post-weaning from the dam. Plasma βHB levels were higher after IHx only at
P11 and P17. This increased in βHB suggests that hepatic ketogenesis was upregulated up to
P17. While peripheral tissue reprogramming after IHx would be an interesting focus for a future
study, in this work, we aimed to delineate metabolic reprogramming in the hippocampus after IHx.
9. IHx group weighs significantly less than Nx at most timepoints in both sexes. I understand this
is necessary to model extremely preterm infants, however, this could also impact overall
metabolism, and substrates used for energy. Are hippocampal lipid alterations a result of hypoxia,
weight loss, or both?
Thank you for your thoughtful comment. As this reviewer pointed out, we observed reduced body
weight gain in the IHx group up to P30 in both sexes. As mentioned above (comment #8), the
blood levels of substrates were maintained (glucose, lactate) or even increased (βHB) indicating
that delivery of substrates for brain energy and metabolism was comparable to Nx controls.
Therefore, these results suggest that hippocampal lipid alterations were not due to a limited
supply of substrates for brain energy and growth.
While substrate delivery was comparable to Nx, the fate of the substrates differ in the IHx group.
In this study, using biochemical and genetic approaches, we demonstrated that following IHx,
astrocytes extensively oxidized long-chain fatty acids – a process that is dismal in the developing
brain – and affected subsequent hippocampal lipid composition.

but what dose would it need to be administered as, and would this be GRAS?
Thank you for this comment. We would like to further clarify that the US Food and Drug
Administration (FDA) classifies glycerol-triacetate as GRAS (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-
21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-184/subpart-B/section-184.1901).
Clinically and in in vivo animal models, acetate cannot be administered on its own; it has to be
delivered as either sodium or potassium acetate and is usually administered intravenously in
humans. The concern is that in very vulnerable extremely preterm infants, the sodium or
potassium may cause a significant metabolic and electrolyte disturbance. Glycerol-triacetate
allows oral administration, is readily absorbed in the gut, and is an FDA compound not associated
with toxicity.
In our study, glycerol-triacetin (Millipore Sigma; 1030001000) was administered via gavage to
ensure that the full dose was given. At the dose that we administered (5mg/g body weight) we did
not see side effects. In order to determine the dose in humans, an IRB approved clinical trial
would be necessary. To bypass the bitter taste that can be associated with glycerol-triacetate,
the compound can be administered by oral gavage, which is often done in the neonatal intensive care
units (NICU).
In a study of two patients with Canavan disease, administration of glycerol-triacetate at 4.5g/kg
was well tolerated (PMID: 21474353)43.

13. The concept of astrocytes being specialized to oxidize fatty acids is well-established (for

The novelty of our study is that this is the first study to report: 1) fatty acid oxidation occurs
specifically in the developing brain following a model of neonatal brain injury due to prematurity,
2) fatty acid oxidation was still present 6 days after the injury during the recovery period under
normoxic conditions, and 3) in vivo administration of glycerol-triacetate significantly reduce
hippocampal fatty acid oxidation by ~71% in the IHx group.

Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Fernandez et al. provides new evidence that during the critical period of brain
development in neonates born extremely prematurely, brain mitochondria increasingly rely on
fatty acid oxidation. This metabolic shift coincides with a reduction in total brain fatty acids and
complex lipid classes, which may contribute to behavioral changes. The authors demonstrate that
supplementation with alternative fuels, such as acetate, in in vivo and in vitro models, spares fatty
acids and leads to improved neurological outcomes. Authors use of intermittent hypoxia as a
model to study neonatal brain injury in extremely preterm infants. Overall, the manuscript is well
presented, and the major conclusions are supported by the data.
The reviewer suggests the following improvements to enhance the clarity and rigor of the
manuscript:
1. Authors need to improve the consistency in Definitions of Fatty Acid Classes. In line 355, the
authors consider very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA) as lipids with more than 22 carbons;
however, in Figures 1J/K (and similarly in Extended Figures 2C/D, 9B/C), the cutoff appears to
be 20 carbons. Can the authors reconcile this discrepancy between the results and conclusions?
For consistency, it is generally accepted that long-chain fatty acids (LCFA) include lipids with 12–
20 carbons, while VLCFA are those with 22–38 carbons. Distinguishing between these two
categories is important, as the data treat all fatty acids similarly, yet the discussion focuses
primarily on VLCFA.
We thank the reviewer for the pointing out this discrepancy. In this revised version of the
manuscript, we corrected both results and discussion sections.
2. Presentation of Lipid Remodeling Data could be also improved. The changes shown in lipid
remodeling of free fatty acids appear modest (Figures 1I, Extended Figures 2B, 4F, 5D, 3C, and
9A), and the graphs make it difficult to discern statistically significant trends. Rather than
displaying all data, including non-significant changes, the authors could provide a comprehensive
table summarizing all results and only depict statistically significant changes in the figures for
clarity.
In this submission, we provide raw data containing total lipid fatty acids and acylcarnitines in excel
format as well as all statistical analyses (Source data and Supplementary Information). However,
to reconcile the critiques from reviewers 3 and 5, we are displaying the results as heatmaps in
the main figure and report percent of fatty acids from total fatty acids in a supplemental table for
all ages and sexes.
3. Could the observed phenotype be explained simply by low body weight and, consequently, a
reduced capacity to accumulate adipose tissue, which is essential for normal brain development?
The authors are encouraged to address this possibility.
We thank the reviewer for this interesting and intriguing point. The brain relies on a constant
supply of substrates for growth, development, and metabolism. This supply is fulfilled by delivery
of these substrates via systemic circulation. Our results show that IHx did not result in
hypoglycemia and did not decrease blood levels of lactate, βHB, and NEFA. At P17, 6 days post-
injury, we continue to observe in the IHx group increased blood levels of βHB generated in the
liver and comparable levels of NEFA to Nx. Indeed, recent elegant studies by Bazinet’s group,
showed that glucose is the primary substrate for de novo lipogenesis in the developing brain
(PMID: 38233416)35. Furthermore, this group demonstrated that mice fed a low palmitic acid
(C16:0 – primary product of de novo lipogenesis) diet, preserved brain palmitic acid levels by
upregulating hepatic synthesis from dietary sugars. We want to point out that neither levels of
brain palmitic acid or essential fatty acids (ω-6 and ω-3) were decreased following IHx at any age
studied. Instead, we observed decreased levels of ≥20 carbon-long saturated and ω-9 fatty acids,
which are synthesize locally (in the brain). Taken together, these results suggest that there was
no compromise in nutrition or circulating levels of substrates for de novo lipogenesis, and the
observed changes are due to disrupted lipid metabolism in the brain.
Clinical observational studies extensively report that newborns born preterm have low birth weight
and are closely monitored for weight gain and growth during subsequent NICU stay. By the age
equivalent to full term newborn (40 weeks), these infants have total adiposity comparable to term
newborns (PMID: 15611357, PMID: 10212079)50,51. Most (~80%) of preterm infants experience
catch up in growth by age 2-3 years, while in the other 20%, this catch up growth can last until
adolescence (PMID: 18953169, PMID: 11044763, PMID: 15795505, PMID: 16291360, PMID:
15033844)52–56. Adults born preterm with very low birth weight, display shorter height and
equivalent adipose tissue compared to those born full term (PMID: 37973945)57. Indeed, our
results show that we recapitulate in mice the clinical observed phenomenon of low body weight
throughout development. Ongoing studies in our lab are further characterizing body fat, lean
mass, and adiposity in our model of IHx using EchoMRI 100 QNMR instrument.
4. The authors report that supplementation with glycerol-triacetate improves neurological
recovery based on NOR scores. Does this treatment also result in improvements in brain lipidomic
profiles, particularly in the hippocampus? Including this data and more presenting more
phenotypic data would strengthen the conclusions.
We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. This revised submission now includes the new results
regarding the effects of glycerol-triacetate on brain lipid composition. Specifically, we report body
and brain weight, hippocampal percent of total lipid per mg of hippocampus, and total
hippocampal lipid fatty acid analysis.
Our results show that treatment with glycerol-triacetate after IHx restored hippocampal total lipid
fatty acid composition. Specifically, the levels of ≥20 carbon-long saturated and ω-9 fatty acids
decreased in the IHx-injured mice group were comparable to the normoxia controls following
treatment with glycerol-triacetate. These data are now reported in figure 7 and supplementary
figure 9.
